events.title_line: University of Connecticut · USA · 2019
events.headline: 49 trials: yoga lowered blood pressure. Adding breathing and relaxation nearly doubled the drop in people with high blood pressure.
events.meaning: The breath is not an extra. Yoga with breathing and relaxation gave the biggest blood pressure drop in these trials.
events.details: Meta-analysis (a study of studies) of 49 controlled trials with 56 yoga programs and 3,517 adults. Average age 49, average starting blood pressure 129/81. Average practice: about 5 sessions a week, 59 minutes each, for 13 weeks. Overall, yoga lowered top (systolic) blood pressure by 5.0 mmHg and bottom (diastolic) by 3.9 mmHg compared with control groups (P<0.001 for both). In the authors' best-case model for groups with high blood pressure practicing 3 times a week, yoga that included breathing techniques and meditation or relaxation lowered blood pressure by about 11/6 mmHg, compared with about 6/3 mmHg for yoga without them. Published in Mayo Clinic Proceedings, March 2019.
events.citation: Wu Y, Johnson BT, Acabchuk RL, Chen S, Lewis HK, Livingston J, Park CL, Pescatello LS. Yoga as antihypertensive lifestyle therapy: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Mayo Clin Proc. 2019;94(3):432-446. doi:10.1016/j.mayocp.2018.09.023. PMID 30792067.
events.caution: The 11/6 number comes from a statistical model of the best case, not from one single trial. Not every trial was randomized. Keep taking blood pressure medicine unless your doctor changes it. People with high blood pressure should breathe softly and avoid straining or hard breath holding. Ask a doctor first.

events.title_line: University of Pavia and Santa Maria Nuova Hospital, Florence · Italy · 2001
events.headline: A rosary or a yoga mantra slowed breathing to about 6 breaths a minute. Blood pressure control got stronger.
events.meaning: Slow, steady breathing near 6 breaths a minute is free and simple. A prayer or a mantra can help set that pace.
events.details: 23 healthy adults (16 men, 7 women, average age 34) in Florence and Pavia, Italy. Researchers measured breathing, heart rhythm, blood pressure and brain blood flow in five states: quiet normal breathing, breathing to a set pace of 6 a minute, free talking, saying the Ave Maria (in Latin), and saying a yoga mantra. Normal quiet breathing was about 14 breaths a minute. The Ave Maria slowed it to 5.6 and the mantra to 5.7, close to one breath every 10 seconds. Breathing became much more even: the change from breath to breath fell from 37% during free talking to 8% with the Ave Maria and 6% with the mantra. The natural waves in heart rate and blood pressure got bigger and moved together. Baroreflex sensitivity (the body's fast blood pressure control) rose from 9.5 ms/mmHg during free talking to 11.5 with the Ave Maria and 12.3 with the mantra (P<0.05). The authors wrote that the rosary might be viewed as a health practice as well as a religious practice. Published in the BMJ, 22 December 2001.
events.citation: Bernardi L, Sleight P, Bandinelli G, Cencetti S, Fattorini L, Wdowczyc-Szulc J, Lagi A. Effect of rosary prayer and yoga mantras on autonomic cardiovascular rhythms: comparative study. BMJ. 2001;323(7327):1446-1449. doi:10.1136/bmj.323.7327.1446. PMID 11751348. PMCID PMC61046. Press release (BMJ Group, 20 Dec 2001): EurekAlert, https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/766123
events.caution: Small study: 23 healthy adults, measured during one lab session, not randomized. It shows body signals changed while people were reciting, not that any disease was prevented or that the effect lasts. Slow the breath gently; never strain or force it. Respectful framing only: present the rosary and the mantra as equals, never mock either.

events.title_line: Centre for Chronic Disease Control and 24 medical centers · India · 2020
events.headline: In 3,959 heart attack patients, gentle yoga with breathing gave small gains in health and getting back to daily life.
events.meaning: Where heart rehab clinics are missing, yoga may be one option. No harm was reported during the yoga sessions.
events.details: Randomized trial in 24 medical centers across India, run with the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine. 3,959 adults after a heart attack. 1,970 got Yoga-CaRe: 13 sessions over 12 weeks, about 75 minutes each, with gentle yoga movement, breath control, meditation and relaxation, led by trained yoga teachers, plus practice at home with booklets and videos. 1,989 got 3 sessions of health advice with a leaflet. Followed for a median of about 22 months. Self-rated health at 12 weeks: 77 vs 75.7 out of 100 (p=0.002). Return to normal daily activities from before the heart attack: score 88.3 vs 87.0 (p=0.039), a small gain. New major heart events: 6.7% vs 7.4%, not a significant difference. Taking medicines and quitting tobacco were the same in both groups. No adverse events were reported during the yoga sessions. Published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology, April 2020.
events.citation: Prabhakaran D, Chandrasekaran AM, Singh K, et al. Yoga-based cardiac rehabilitation after acute myocardial infarction: a randomized trial. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2020;75(13):1551-1561. doi:10.1016/j.jacc.2020.01.050. PMID 32241371. Full text: PMC7132532.
events.caution: The gains were small. The trial did not show that yoga prevents new heart events; it was too small to test that. Start only after your heart team says it is safe, and keep taking your heart medicines.

events.topic: Heart rhythm: yoga and atrial fibrillation
events.title_line: University of Kansas Hospital · Kansas City, USA · 2013
events.headline: After 3 months of yoga, people with an irregular heartbeat had fewer episodes: 2.1 instead of 3.8 on average.
events.meaning: In this small study, people who added yoga to their normal heart care had fewer episodes and less anxiety and depression.
events.details: YOGA My Heart Study, one hospital, no separate control group. 52 adults with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (AF that comes and goes) enrolled and 49 finished (47% men, average age 61, AF for about 5 years, 78% on rhythm medicine). Each person was compared with themselves. First 3 months: normal life, no yoga. Next 3 months: Iyengar yoga with breathing, asana, meditation and relaxation, 60 minutes, at least twice a week. Results, yoga months vs the months before: symptom AF episodes fell from 3.8 to 2.1 (p<0.001). Other symptom heartbeat episodes fell from 2.9 to 1.4 (p<0.001). Silent AF episodes fell from 0.12 to 0.04 (p<0.001). Heart rate, top and bottom blood pressure all went down (p<0.001). Anxiety and depression scores dropped (p<0.001). Physical function, general health, vitality, social life and mental health scores went up. Published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology, March 2013.
events.citation: Lakkireddy D, Atkins D, Pillarisetti J, Ryschon K, Bommana S, Drisko J, Vanga S, Dawn B. Effect of yoga on arrhythmia burden, anxiety, depression, and quality of life in paroxysmal atrial fibrillation: the YOGA My Heart Study. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2013;61(11):1177-1182. doi:10.1016/j.jacc.2012.11.060. PMID 23375926. Enrolment, age, sex and medicine figures: ACC expert analysis, https://www.acc.org/latest-in-cardiology/articles/2014/07/18/17/24/yoga-for-paroxysmal-atrial-fibrillation-an-ancient-solution-to-an-emerging-problem. Lead doctor quote on blood thinners: Medical News Today, https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/221105
events.caution: Small study at one hospital (49 people), not randomized, no separate control group: people were compared with their own earlier 3 months, so it cannot prove yoga caused the change. Lead doctor Dhanunjaya Lakkireddy said yoga is strictly a supplement to medical care and patients should not stop their blood thinners. Ask your heart doctor before starting. Some news stories say 3 sessions a week of 45 minutes; the published paper says twice a week, 60 minutes, so use twice a week.

events.topic: Strong lungs, strong heart: breathing muscle training
events.title_line: University of Colorado Boulder · USA · 2021
events.headline: Just 30 hard breaths a day through a small device lowered top blood pressure by 9 points in 6 weeks.
events.meaning: Your breathing muscles can be trained like legs. Training them helped blood vessels and blood pressure in adults aged 50 to 79.
events.details: Double-blind randomized trial with a fake (sham) group. 36 adults aged 50 to 79 with top blood pressure of 120 or higher. They breathed in hard through a small hand-held device that pushes back, 30 breaths a day, 6 days a week, for 6 weeks (about 5 minutes a day). Real group (n=18) trained at 75% of their max breathing-in strength. Sham group (n=18) trained at only 15%, and nobody knew which group they were in. Real group: top blood pressure fell from 135 to 126 mmHg (P<0.01). Bottom number fell a little, from 79 to 77 mmHg (P=0.03). About 75% of the drop was still there 6 weeks after they stopped. 24-hour top blood pressure was also lower than in the sham group. Blood vessel function (flow-mediated dilation) improved about 45%. Sham group: no real change in blood pressure or blood vessel function. Artery stiffness did not change in either group. People completed about 95% of sessions. CU Boulder said the 9-point drop was generally bigger than what walking 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week gives, and about the same as some blood pressure drug plans. The method was first made in the 1980s to help very sick lung patients make their breathing muscles stronger. Published online in the Journal of the American Heart Association on 29 June 2021 (issue of July 2021).
events.citation: Craighead DH, Heinbockel TC, Freeberg KA, Rossman MJ, et al., Seals DR. Time-efficient inspiratory muscle strength training lowers blood pressure and improves endothelial function, NO bioavailability, and oxidative stress in midlife/older adults with above-normal blood pressure. J Am Heart Assoc. 2021;10(13):e020980. doi:10.1161/JAHA.121.020980. PMID 34184544. Trial NCT03266510. Press release: https://www.colorado.edu/today/2021/06/29/5-minute-breathing-workout-lowers-blood-pressure-much-exercise-drugs
events.caution: This used a resistance breathing device (inspiratory muscle training), not yoga pranayama, so do not say pranayama did this. Small study, 36 people, aged 50 to 79, only 6 weeks. Anyone with heart or lung disease, or on blood pressure medicine, should ask a doctor before strong breathing training.

events.title_line: Cochrane review, Chinese University of Hong Kong · 2016
events.headline: 15 trials, 1,048 people with asthma: yoga probably gave small gains in quality of life and symptoms.
events.meaning: A top medical review found small gains, not final proof. Use yoga next to asthma medicine, never instead of it.
events.details: Zuyao Yang and team pooled 15 randomized trials with 1,048 people. Most were adults with mild to moderate asthma. 8 trials were in India, 3 in the USA, 2 in the UK, 1 in Germany and 1 in Ethiopia. Programs lasted 2 weeks to 54 months, most up to 6 months. 5 trials used yoga breathing only. The other 10 mixed breathing, asana and meditation. Quality of life score went up 0.57 points more than in the other groups, on a 7 point scale (5 trials, 375 people). That is more than the 0.5 points doctors count as a real change. Symptoms got a little better (3 trials, 243 people). The lung blow test (FEV1) did not clearly change: plus 0.04 litres, not significant (7 trials, 340 people). No serious side effects were reported, but data was limited. The review rated the quality of life and symptom results moderate quality, and the lung test and safety results very low quality. The authors called the results early signs, not final proof.
events.citation: Yang ZY, Zhong HB, Mao C, Yuan JQ, Huang YF, Wu XY, Gao YM, Tang JL. Yoga for asthma. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2016;(4):CD010346. doi:10.1002/14651858.CD010346.pub2. PMID 27115477.
events.caution: Yoga did not clearly change the lung test number (FEV1). In 2 trials that used a fake breathing method for comparison, quality of life did not clearly improve. Keep taking asthma medicine as your doctor says, and keep your inhaler near your mat.

events.title_line: University of Duisburg-Essen, Germany · 2019
events.headline: 11 trials, 586 people with COPD, a long-term lung disease: yoga helped them walk farther and breathe out more air.
events.meaning: Sick lungs can work a little better with practice. Gains showed up only in breathing-focused yoga (pranayama), not programs with asana.
events.details: Holger Cramer and team pooled 11 randomized trials with 586 people with COPD, a long-term lung disease that makes breathing hard. Compared with no treatment, people who did yoga walked about 25.5 meters farther in a 6 minute walk test. Lung function (FEV1, the air you can blow out in 1 second) rose by about 4 percentage points of the expected value for their body (3.95%). Quality of life also improved (3.81 points on the COPD Assessment Test), but that result was less solid and did not hold up when weaker studies were checked. The surprise: the gains showed up only in breathing-focused yoga, not in programs that included asana. Few trials reported on side effects, so the authors say safety needs more study. An earlier review (Liu and team, Shandong University, China, 2014, 5 trials, 233 patients) found FEV1 up about 124 mL and walking up about 39 meters.
events.citation: Cramer H, Haller H, Klose P, Ward L, Chung VC, Lauche R. The risks and benefits of yoga for patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Clinical Rehabilitation. 2019;33(12):1847-1862. doi:10.1177/0269215519860551. PMID 31353959. Also: Liu XC, Pan L, Hu Q, Dong WP, Yan JH, Dong L. Effects of yoga training in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Thorac Dis. 2014;6(6):795-802. doi:10.3978/j.issn.2072-1439.2014.06.05. PMID 24977005.
events.caution: Yoga breathing is an add-on to lung rehab and medicine, not a swap. People with COPD should ask their doctor before strong or fast breathing practices.

events.title_line: Stanford University · 2023
events.headline: In 108 adults, 5 minutes a day of long, slow out-breaths lifted good mood more than meditation did.
events.meaning: You do not need an hour. Five minutes of long, slow out-breaths is a free tool you can carry everywhere.
events.details: Randomized controlled trial run fully at home (remote) in 2020 by Stanford School of Medicine (Spiegel and Huberman labs). 108 adults aged 18 and over, 5 minutes per day, for 28 days. Four groups: cyclic sighing (30 people: breathe in through the nose, then a second short breath in to fill the lungs, then a slow full breath out through the mouth), box breathing (21), fast breathing with breath holds (33), and mindfulness meditation (24). Average daily rise in good mood (PANAS scale, 10 to 50): 1.91 points for the three breathing groups together vs 1.22 for meditation (cyclic sighing 1.89, fast breathing 1.97, box breathing 1.84). In the study's main model, cyclic sighing was the best at lifting mood over the month, and the gain grew the more days people practiced. Only cyclic sighing lowered resting breathing rate clearly more than meditation, measured each day by a wrist strap. People whose breathing rate dropped the most also had the biggest mood lift (r = -0.24). All four groups felt less anxious and less bad mood right after each session. The authors think, but did not test, that part of the calming effect may travel through the vagus nerve, which links brain, heart and lungs.
events.citation: Balban MY, Neri E, Kogon MM, Weed L, Nouriani B, Jo B, Holl G, Zeitzer JM, Spiegel D, Huberman AD. Brief structured respiration practices enhance mood and reduce physiological arousal. Cell Rep Med. 2023;4(1):100895. doi:10.1016/j.xcrm.2022.100895. PMID 36630953. PMCID PMC9873947. Trial NCT05304000.
events.caution: One small trial, mostly healthy adults, done at home, so nobody checked how people really practiced. Meditation lowered anxiety and bad mood just as well; breathing only won on good mood. Heart rate variability, resting heart rate, sleep and long-term anxiety did not change. One author (Huberman) advises WHOOP, the company that made the wrist strap. The study left out people with heart disease, glaucoma, seizures, pregnancy, bipolar disorder, psychosis or serious mental illness, so those people should ask a doctor first, especially before fast breathing with breath holds.

events.title_line: University of Sussex & University of Oxford, UK · 2023
events.headline: In 12 trials with 785 adults, breathing practice lowered stress. More trials found less anxiety and depression too.
events.meaning: Slow breathing, as in pranayama, now has support from trials: it helped lower stress by a small to medium amount.
events.details: Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, searched up to February 2022 (1,325 records found at first). Stress: 12 trials, 785 adults (417 did breathwork, 368 were in control groups). People who did breathwork had lower stress than control groups (effect size g = -0.35, small to medium, p = 0.0009). Anxiety: 20 trials, g = -0.32. Depressive symptoms: 18 trials, g = -0.40. Of the 12 stress trials, 10 taught slow breathing and 2 taught fast breathing. 6 were in people with a physical illness, 5 in people without illness, and 1 in a mental health group. The clear drop in stress showed up with slow breathing and in people without illness. For fast breathing and for patient groups the result was not clear, because there were few studies. Estimated minimum practice time ranged from 80 to 5,625 minutes in total. Half of the stress trials were self-help, with no live teacher. Four stress trials (six in all) checked for harm. None reported adverse events or lasting bad effects caused by the breathing.
events.citation: Fincham GW, Strauss C, Montero-Marin J, Cavanagh K. Effect of breathwork on stress and mental health: a meta-analysis of randomised-controlled trials. Sci Rep. 2023;13(1):432. doi:10.1038/s41598-022-27247-y. PMID 36624160. PMCID PMC9828383.
events.caution: Most trials were small and had a moderate risk of bias. The authors say breathwork 'may be' effective and warn against hype. For people with a physical or mental illness the stress result was not clear, so the authors say it is too early to recommend it as treatment there. Only adults were studied. In one fast-breathing depression study, a small group felt hot flushes, shortness of breath or sweating. They chose to keep going and no one quit because of it. Fast breathing (like kapalabhati) needs advice first in pregnancy, epilepsy, heart problems or panic attacks. If you feel dizzy, stop and breathe normally.

events.title_line: University of South Australia & UNSW Sydney · 2020
events.headline: 13 trials, 632 people with mental health conditions: moving yoga lowered depression symptoms. More sessions each week, bigger drops.
events.meaning: Showing up often may matter. Trials with more yoga sessions each week saw bigger drops in depression symptoms.
events.details: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (search up to 14 May 2019). Authors from University of South Australia, UNSW Sydney, Federal University of Santa Maria (Brazil), King's College London and University of Manchester. Only physically active yoga counted: at least 50% of each session spent moving, holding asana and flowing through sequences. The review found 19 trials with 1,080 adults who had a diagnosed mental disorder (depression, PTSD, schizophrenia, anxiety, alcohol dependence, bipolar disorder). 13 trials (632 people) were pooled: yoga lowered depressive symptoms more than waitlist, usual care or attention control (standardized mean difference 0.41, p < 0.001). Trials with more yoga sessions per week showed bigger drops (beta = -0.44, p < 0.01). UNSW's Simon Rosenbaum: 'The more sessions per week people engaged in, the greater the benefit was.'
events.citation: Brinsley J, Schuch F, Lederman O, Girard D, Smout M, Immink MA, Stubbs B, Firth J, Davison K, Rosenbaum S. Effects of yoga on depressive symptoms in people with mental disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med. 2021;55(17):992-1000 (online 18 May 2020). doi:10.1136/bjsports-2019-101242. PMID 32423912.
events.caution: The pooled trials were small, about 49 people each on average. The link between more sessions and bigger drops compares trials, so it is not proof for each person. The researchers say more data is needed on yoga type, intensity and breathing. Yoga here was compared with waitlist, usual care or attention control, so keep any doctor-led treatment going.

events.title_line: Beijing University of Chinese Medicine · China · 2025
events.headline: 22 trials: adults with insomnia who did yoga reported almost 2 more hours of sleep a night.
events.meaning: Yoga may be a low cost, gentle way to help sleep. Use it next to your doctor's advice, not instead of it.
events.details: Scientists pooled 22 randomized trials with 1,348 adults with insomnia. They compared 13 treatments, and 7 of them were exercise: yoga, tai chi, walking or jogging, strength training, and other types. Programs lasted 4 to 26 weeks. Compared with people given usual care or lifestyle advice, people who did yoga wrote down in sleep diaries about 111 more minutes of sleep a night. The share of time in bed spent asleep went up by about 15.6 points. Time awake in the night dropped by about 56 minutes, and people fell asleep about 29 minutes faster. Tai chi and walking or jogging also helped. The authors found yoga, tai chi and walking or jogging worked better than the other exercises. Published online 15 July 2025 in BMJ Evidence-Based Medicine (print issue 2026).
events.citation: Bu ZJ, Liu FS, Shahjalal M, et al. Effects of various exercise interventions in insomnia patients: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. BMJ Evid Based Med. 2026;31(2):102-113. Published online 15 July 2025. doi:10.1136/bmjebm-2024-113512. PMID 40664502.
events.caution: The yoga numbers come from sleep diaries people filled in, not sleep lab machines. The authors rated certainty as moderate for total sleep time and low for the other yoga results. Only 4 of the 22 trials were rated low risk of bias, and the authors say bigger, better trials are needed. Long insomnia can have medical causes, so people should also see a doctor. Say yoga 'helped', never that it fixes insomnia.

events.title_line: Northwestern University · Chicago, USA · 2016
events.headline: People picked out pictures they had seen before more accurately while breathing in through the nose. Not through the mouth.
events.meaning: Ashtanga asks for steady nose breathing. This study found brain waves in memory and feeling areas move with the nose breath.
events.details: Christina Zelano and Jay Gottfried's team first studied 7 people with epilepsy who already had electrodes in their brains, placed to find where seizures started before surgery. Brain waves in the smell area, the amygdala (fear and feeling) and the hippocampus (memory) moved in time with the breath. They were strongest on the in-breath. In 3 of these patients, the waves faded when they breathed through the mouth. Then healthy young adults, ages 18 to 30, did two lab tests. Fear test (70 people): they spotted fearful faces faster when the face came on a nose in-breath than on an out-breath. Surprised faces showed no change. Memory test (42 people): they saw pictures of objects, then later picked out the ones they had seen before. They were more accurate when the test picture came on a nose in-breath. The breath phase when they first saw the picture did not matter. These effects were not seen in the groups who breathed through the mouth. Published in the Journal of Neuroscience, 7 December 2016.
events.citation: Zelano C, Jiang H, Zhou G, Arora N, Schuele S, Rosenow J, Gottfried JA. Nasal Respiration Entrains Human Limbic Oscillations and Modulates Cognitive Function. J Neurosci. 2016;36(49):12448-12467. doi:10.1523/JNEUROSCI.2586-16.2016. PMID 27927961. PMCID PMC5148230. Press release: https://news.northwestern.edu/stories/2016/12/rhythm-of-breathing-affects-memory-and-fear
events.caution: Small lab study. The memory test was a short picture test, not long-term memory, and the healthy people were only 18 to 30 years old. It does not show nose breathing treats memory problems or anxiety. The patients were not named; keep it that way. People with a blocked nose should not force nose breathing.

events.title_line: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign · USA · 2014
events.headline: 118 adults, average age 62: after 8 weeks, yoga beat stretching on working memory and task-switching tests.
events.meaning: Starting in your 60s still counts. Three 1-hour classes a week for 8 weeks helped thinking skills, not only the body.
events.details: Neha Gothe, Arthur Kramer and Edward McAuley split 118 adults (average age 62) by chance: 61 to Hatha yoga and 57 to a stretching and strengthening class. Both groups had 1-hour classes 3 times a week for 8 weeks. Yoga classes included asana, sun salutations, alternate nostril breathing and meditation. 108 people finished, and both groups came to about 81% of classes. The yoga group got faster at switching between tasks and more accurate on working memory tests (the 2-back test and part of a memory span test) than the stretching group. Published online July 2014, in the September 2014 issue of the Journal of Gerontology: Medical Sciences.
events.citation: Gothe NP, Kramer AF, McAuley E. The effects of an 8-week Hatha yoga intervention on executive function in older adults. J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci. 2014;69(9):1109-1116. doi:10.1093/gerona/glu095. PMID 25024234. PMCID PMC4202261.
events.caution: The gains were small to medium and were tested right after the 8 weeks, so we do not know how long they last. One memory score (total recall) did not change enough to count. Most people in the study were white women who did not exercise much before. It was not a dementia study. Older beginners should modify asana; people with glaucoma or high blood pressure should skip headstand and other upside-down asana unless their doctor says it is OK.

events.title_line: University of Rochester (YOCAS trial) · USA · 2013
events.headline: In a 410-person trial, 4 weeks of gentle yoga helped cancer survivors sleep better and use fewer sleeping pills.
events.meaning: Gentle breathing, soft asana and rest helped adults sleep better after cancer treatment. Older survivors said it helped too.
events.details: 410 adult cancer survivors who slept badly, 2 to 24 months after surgery, chemo or radiation (96% women, average age 54, 75% breast cancer). Run by 9 community cancer programs in 12 US cities, 2007 to 2010. Chosen by chance: 206 got yoga plus usual care, 204 got usual care only. Yoga: 2 classes a week, 75 minutes each, for 4 weeks, in small groups of about 12. Each class had pranayama (breathing), 16 gentle Hatha and restorative asanas, and meditation. Results (people with full data, 168 yoga and 153 usual care): the sleep problem score (lower is better) dropped 1.96 points (9.2 to 7.2) with yoga vs 1.07 points with usual care. Sleeping pill use went down 21% per week in the yoga group but went up 5% per week in the usual care group. The yoga group also had fewer daytime problems and spent less time awake at night (measured by a wrist sleep tracker). 90% said yoga helped their sleep. A 2024 look at the same trial (177 people from the yoga group with full data): those aged 60 and over had less tiredness too, like the younger ones, and 88.5% of the older group said yoga helped their sleep.
events.citation: Mustian KM, Sprod LK, Janelsins M, Peppone LJ, Palesh OG, Chandwani K, Reddy PS, Melnik MK, Heckler C, Morrow GR. Multicenter, randomized controlled trial of yoga for sleep quality among cancer survivors. J Clin Oncol. 2013;31(26):3233-3241. doi:10.1200/JCO.2012.43.7707. PMID 23940231. PMCID PMC3757292. Follow up (yoga group only): Arana-Chicas E, Lin PJ, Gada U, et al. The effect of YOCAS yoga on cancer-related fatigue and quality of life in older (60+) vs. younger (59 and under) cancer survivors: secondary analysis of a nationwide, multicenter, phase 3 randomized controlled trial. J Geriatr Oncol. 2024;15(8):102076. doi:10.1016/j.jgo.2024.102076. PMID 39368335.
events.caution: Most people were women with breast cancer, and 22% did not give full data. Sleep got better in both groups; the extra gain from yoga was under 1 point on the score. The yoga was gentle Hatha and restorative, not a full Ashtanga series. It helped sleep and tiredness only; it does not treat the cancer itself. Anyone still in treatment should ask their cancer doctor first.

events.topic: Cancer patients and survivors: fatigue and inflammation
events.title_line: Ohio State University · USA · 2014
events.headline: Breast cancer survivors who did yoga had 57% less tiredness and less inflammation than a no-yoga group, months later.
events.meaning: The benefit was bigger 3 months after classes ended. The lead scientist thinks the breathing and meditation parts were really important.
events.details: 200 breast cancer survivors, ages 27 to 76, stage 0 to 3A, who had finished surgery or radiation 2 months to 3 years before. 100 women did Hatha yoga classes 2 times a week, 90 minutes each, for 12 weeks, and were asked to practice at home too. 100 women were on a wait list and did no yoga during the study. Right after the 12 weeks: the yoga group had a 12% higher vitality (energy) score. 3 months after classes ended (6 months into the study): fatigue was 57% lower than in the no-yoga group. When their blood cells were tested in the lab, they made 13 to 20% less of 3 inflammation proteins (IL-6, TNF-alpha, IL-1 beta). Women who practiced more often got bigger changes. The yoga group also slept better. Lead scientist Janice Kiecolt-Glaser: "We think the breathing and meditation components were really important in terms of some of the changes we were seeing."
events.citation: Kiecolt-Glaser JK, Bennett JM, Andridge R, et al. Yoga's impact on inflammation, mood, and fatigue in breast cancer survivors: a randomized controlled trial. J Clin Oncol. 2014;32(10):1040-1049. doi:10.1200/JCO.2013.51.8860. PMID 24470004. PMCID PMC3965259. Numbers from Ohio State News release, 26 January 2014.
events.caution: Right after the 12 weeks, the drop in fatigue was not yet clear by statistics. The big difference showed 3 months later. Depression scores did not differ between groups. The no-yoga group got no other class, so part of the effect may come from attention and group support (the authors say this). Tiredness was self-reported. The 57% and 13 to 20% numbers come from the Ohio State news release. This helped side effects and wellbeing only, not the cancer itself.

events.topic: Cancer patients and survivors: yoga vs stretching during radiation
events.title_line: MD Anderson Cancer Center with VYASA (Bengaluru, India) · Houston, USA · 2014
events.headline: During breast cancer radiation, yoga helped women with daily tasks more than stretching did, even 6 months later.
events.meaning: A yoga class mixing asanas, breathing, relaxation and meditation gave extra help beyond stretching. The study cannot say which part mattered most.
events.details: 163 women with breast cancer (stage 0 to 3), about to start 6 weeks of radiation, were split by chance into 3 groups: yoga (53 women), simple stretching (56) or waiting list (54). Yoga and stretching classes were up to 3 times a week, 60 minutes each. The yoga class had a warm up linked to the breath, gentle asanas (bending forward, back and sideways, cobra, crocodile, and a supported half shoulder stand), deep relaxation lying down, alternate nostril breathing (pranayama) and meditation. Teachers were trained by VYASA in Bengaluru, India. Stretching was taught by MD Anderson physiotherapists. Results: at 1, 3 and 6 months after radiation, the yoga group reported better physical functioning (daily tasks like walking, lifting and climbing stairs) than BOTH the stretching group and the waiting group. By the end of radiation, yoga and stretching both lowered fatigue more than waiting. In saliva tests, the yoga group's stress hormone (cortisol) fell more steeply from morning to night at the end of radiation and 1 month later, a daily rhythm scientists link to better health.
events.citation: Chandwani KD, Perkins G, Nagendra HR, et al. Randomized, controlled trial of yoga in women with breast cancer undergoing radiotherapy. J Clin Oncol. 2014;32(10):1058-1065. doi:10.1200/JCO.2012.48.2752. PMID 24590636. PMCID PMC3965260.
events.caution: Yoga did not beat stretching or waiting for mood, depression or sleep scores. This was one hospital, and results come from the women who finished the tests. The class used a supported half shoulder stand: after breast surgery, with a chest port, arm swelling (lymphedema), cancer in the bones or low blood counts, inversions and strong asanas should be changed or skipped. Ask the cancer team first.

events.topic: Cancer patients and survivors: official doctor guideline
events.title_line: Society for Integrative Oncology and ASCO · USA and Canada · 2023
events.headline: Top cancer doctor groups (ASCO and SIO) say yoga may be offered for anxiety and depression in people with cancer.
events.meaning: Yoga is now part of official cancer care advice. Doctors can offer it next to medical treatment, not instead of it.
events.details: In 2023, an expert panel from the Society for Integrative Oncology and the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO), with Linda Carlson of the University of Calgary as lead author, looked at 110 studies: 30 systematic reviews and 80 randomized trials, published from 1990 to 2023. Yoga was recommended for anxiety during and after cancer treatment, and for depression during and after treatment. The best proof was for people with breast cancer: yoga during treatment got a moderate strength recommendation. For other cancers, the advice for yoga was weak, because there were fewer good studies. In 2024, a second ASCO and SIO guideline on cancer tiredness (fatigue) looked at 113 randomized trials from 2013 to 2023. It said yoga may be recommended for fatigue after treatment ends. It also said doctors should not recommend antidepressants or wakefulness drugs to manage cancer fatigue.
events.citation: Carlson LE, Ismaila N, Addington EL, et al. Integrative Oncology Care of Symptoms of Anxiety and Depression in Adults With Cancer: Society for Integrative Oncology-ASCO Guideline. J Clin Oncol. 2023;41(28):4562-4591. doi:10.1200/JCO.23.00857. PMID 37582238. Also: Bower JE, Lacchetti C, Alici Y, et al. Management of Fatigue in Adult Survivors of Cancer: ASCO-Society for Integrative Oncology Guideline Update. J Clin Oncol. 2024;42(20):2456-2487. doi:10.1200/JCO.24.00541. PMID 38754041.
events.caution: The guideline puts yoga next to medical care, never in place of it. Most of the proof comes from women with breast cancer, and many trials had no active comparison group. The panels rated the proof for these therapies as low to moderate quality. Teachers should adapt practice to each body and follow the advice of the patient's doctor.

events.title_line: National Taiwan University Hospital and partners · Taiwan · 2024
events.headline: After 8 weeks of yoga, period pain was 2.75 points lower (out of 10) than with no exercise.
events.meaning: A steady practice may make painful periods easier. Slow, calm relaxation work helped the most, and fewer people quit it.
events.details: A big review (network meta-analysis) joined 29 randomized trials with 1,808 people with period pain. Almost all were young women and teen girls aged 15 to 26. Pain was scored on a 0 to 10 line. Each exercise group was compared with a group that did no exercise program (nothing or usual care). After 8 weeks, yoga lowered pain by 2.75 points more than no exercise. After 4 weeks the yoga drop was 1.63 points, and that result only just counted as real. Other movement also helped after 8 weeks: aerobic exercise 2.77 points, strength training 3.17 points, mixed exercise 3.67 points, and relaxation exercise 3.87 points, the biggest drop. Relaxation exercise meant slow muscle relaxation or belly self massage, and it was the only type where fewer people quit than in the no exercise group. The yoga number came from 5 small trials (about 197 people in yoga groups) from Iran, Japan, Turkey and Egypt. Yoga programs ran from 8 minutes a day to 60 minutes three times a week. Authors' conclusion: all exercise types lowered period pain after 8 weeks.
events.citation: Tsai IC, Hsu CW, Chang CH, Lei WT, Tseng PT, Chang KV. Comparative Effectiveness of Different Exercises for Reducing Pain Intensity in Primary Dysmenorrhea: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Sports Medicine - Open, 2024;10:63. DOI: 10.1186/s40798-024-00718-4
events.caution: The yoga result rests on only 5 small trials, so the number is not exact. The review did not grade evidence quality, and more than half of the trials had some risk of bias. Almost everyone studied was 15 to 26, so we know less about older women. A 2019 Cochrane review (Armour et al., 12 trials, 854 women; DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD004142.pub4) agrees: exercise such as yoga, stretching or aerobics, about 45 to 60 minutes, 3 times a week or more, may cut period pain by about 25 points out of 100 compared with no exercise, but it rated the evidence low quality. Very strong pain, or pain that gets worse over the years, should be checked by a doctor (it can be a sign of endometriosis).

events.topic: Women: PMS (mood and body changes before a period)
events.title_line: University of Birmingham and Loughborough University · UK · 2020
events.headline: 15 trials, 717 women: regular exercise, yoga included, eased PMS, the hard days before a period.
events.meaning: The tired, cranky, teary days before a period may get lighter when you move your body regularly.
events.details: UK researchers joined 15 randomized trials with 717 women (average ages 17 to 34). Programs were about 3 times a week, 30 to 60 minutes each, for 8 to 12 weeks. Types: aerobic exercise, yoga (2 trials), Pilates, water aerobics, stretching and resistance work. Each was compared with a group that did no exercise. Total PMS score (7 trials, 265 women) dropped a lot (standardized difference -1.08). Mood symptoms (8 trials, 427 women) -1.67. Body symptoms (7 trials, 397 women) -1.62. Behavior symptoms (only 2 trials, 92 women) -1.94. Strength of evidence was rated moderate. Authors' words: exercise may be an effective treatment for PMS, but some uncertainty remains.
events.citation: Pearce E, Jolly K, Jones LL, Matthewman G, Zanganeh M, Daley A. Exercise for premenstrual syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. BJGP Open, 2020;4(3). DOI: 10.3399/bjgpopen20X101032
events.caution: Most trials were small, 12 of 15 came from Iran, and 13 of 15 had a high risk of bias. Results varied a lot between trials. Only 2 trials tested yoga, so say 'exercise like yoga'. Very low mood, anger or hopeless feelings before periods (PMDD) need a doctor, not only practice.

events.title_line: University of Duisburg-Essen and University of Technology Sydney · Germany and Australia · 2018
events.headline: 13 trials, 1,306 women: yoga eased menopause symptoms, like low mood and body aches, about as much as other exercise.
events.meaning: Regular yoga may make midlife easier on mood and body. The proof for hot flashes is still weak.
events.details: Review and meta-analysis of 13 randomized trials with 1,306 women (studies searched up to February 2017). Compared with no treatment, yoga lowered total menopause symptoms by a large amount (effect size -1.05), mood and mind symptoms (-0.75), body symptoms like aches (-0.65), hot flashes and night sweats (-0.76), and urinary and vaginal symptoms (-0.53). Compared with other exercise, yoga was about the same for most symptoms. The only extra benefit was a small to medium drop in hot flashes (-0.45). No serious side effects were reported. Authors: yoga seems effective and safe for menopause symptoms, with effects like other exercise.
events.citation: Cramer H, Peng W, Lauche R. Yoga for menopausal symptoms: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Maturitas, 2018;109:13-25. DOI: 10.1016/j.maturitas.2017.12.005 (PubMed 29452777)
events.caution: The results were less sure in trials where the people scoring the results knew who did yoga, or where many women dropped out. The Menopause Society (2023 position statement) does not recommend yoga as a treatment for hot flashes, saying the evidence is too weak. Say 'helped symptoms and mood', not 'stops hot flashes'. Yoga is not a replacement for seeing a doctor.

events.title_line: Tulane University · New Orleans, USA · 2018
events.headline: Worried third graders who did breathing, relaxation and kid asanas, some from Ashtanga, before school felt better in 8 weeks.
events.meaning: A short practice before class may help a worried child. Ten 40-minute sessions showed a change in this small study.
events.details: Randomized controlled trial at one public elementary school in New Orleans. 52 third graders who screened positive for anxiety symptoms on the SCARED test were randomized one by one: 20 got yoga, 32 got usual care (counseling and other activities with the school social worker). Yoga group: 10 small-group sessions, 40 minutes each (400 minutes total), in an empty classroom before the school day, over 8 weeks. One group of 10 kids did it in the fall and another 10 in the spring (the study ran Oct 2016 to Feb 2017). Sessions used the Yoga Ed curriculum: breathing exercises, guided relaxation, and 'several Vinyasa and Ashtanga' asanas made for third graders, led by an experienced children's yoga teacher. Kids filled in the PedsQL quality of life survey about their own feelings. Result: the emotional score went UP 18.27 points in the yoga group and DOWN 0.86 points in the usual care group (p = 0.009). In the adjusted model: +14.17 emotional score (p = 0.001) and +7.43 psychosocial score (p = 0.01). Physical, social and school scores did not change in a statistically significant way. Teachers who got 2 training sessions said they used yoga in class more often (from 1.28 to 2.39 times a week, p = 0.03).
events.citation: Bazzano AN, Anderson CE, Hylton C, Gustat J. Effect of mindfulness and yoga on quality of life for elementary school students and teachers: results of a randomized controlled school-based study. Psychology Research and Behavior Management. 2018;11:81-89. doi:10.2147/PRBM.S157503. PMID 29695937. Tulane press release, Apr 2018: https://news.tulane.edu/pr/school-based-yoga-can-help-children-better-manage-stress-and-anxiety
events.caution: Small study at one school: only 20 kids in the yoga group, and the two yoga groups did it at different times of the year. Breathing, relaxation and asanas were mixed together, so we cannot say which part helped, or that Ashtanga itself was the key. Kids rated their own feelings; it measured quality of life scores, not a medical diagnosis. Physical, social and school scores did not improve significantly. The teacher numbers were self-reported and not part of the randomized test. Yoga can add to, but not replace, help from a counselor or doctor for an anxious child.

events.title_line: Cochrane Review, Beggs and team · Hobart, Australia · 2013
events.headline: Kids with stable asthma who swam 6 to 12 weeks got fitter, and their lungs worked a little better.
events.meaning: Stable asthma need not stop kids moving. Swimming did not make asthma worse. Keep medicine and ask the doctor first.
events.details: Cochrane systematic review led by a team at Royal Hobart Hospital, Australia. It pooled 8 randomized trials with 262 children and teens aged 5 to 18 with stable asthma, mild to severe. In 7 trials, kids swam 30 to 90 minutes, 2 to 3 times a week, for 6 to 12 weeks. In 1 trial they swam 30 minutes, 6 times a week. Control groups had usual care (7 trials) or played golf (1 trial). Fitness: VO2max (how much oxygen the body can use) rose by 9.67 mL/kg/min compared with usual care (2 trials, 32 kids). Other fitness tests rose by a similar amount (4 trials, 74 kids). Lungs: FEV1 (how much air you can blow out in 1 second) rose by about 8 points of percent predicted (8.07), which the authors called a small gain. Based on limited data, swimming did not harm asthma control or cause more attacks, and few asthma problems were reported. The authors rated the fitness gain as high-strength evidence and the lung gain as moderate-strength evidence, and said swimming was well tolerated.
events.citation: Beggs S, Foong YC, Le HC, Noor D, Wood-Baker R, Walters JA. Swimming training for asthma in children and adolescents aged 18 years and under. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2013;(4):CD009607. doi:10.1002/14651858.CD009607.pub2. PMID 23633375. Related: Das RR, Sankar J, Kabra SK. Role of breathing exercises and yoga/pranayama in childhood asthma: a systematic review. Curr Pediatr Rev. 2019;15(3):175-183. doi:10.2174/1573396315666190121122452. PMID 30663571.
events.caution: Swimming did NOT improve asthma control, asthma attacks, quality of life or steroid use. The trials were small, and 3 of them had many kids drop out. The review could not tell if swimming is better than other sports. Pool chlorine was unknown in 4 trials, so ask a doctor about indoor chlorinated pools. Kids must keep taking their asthma medicine and carry their reliever inhaler. A separate review of breathing exercises and yoga/pranayama for asthmatic kids (Das 2019, 10 trials, 466 kids aged 6 to 14) found mixed results and said it cannot yet be a standard treatment, so we cannot claim pranayama alone helps asthma.

events.title_line: Oregon State University · USA · 2001 and 2008
events.headline: Kids who jumped for 7 months still had more hip bone than kids who stretched, almost 8 years later.
events.meaning: Childhood is a key time to build bone. Stretching did not build bone like jumping did, so let kids jump too.
events.details: Randomized trial (Fuchs 2001, Corvallis, Oregon): 89 children aged 5.9 to 9.8, before puberty, split into a jumping group (45) and a stretching group (44). Both groups trained at school 3 days a week for 7 months. Jumpers built up to 100 two-footed jumps off a 61 cm (24 inch) box each session; landings hit about 8 times body weight. The stretching group did no-impact stretching on the same schedule. After 7 months, jumpers gained 4.5% more bone mineral at the hip (femoral neck) and 3.1% more at the lower spine than the stretching group. Height, weight and body fat grew the same in both groups. Follow-up (Gunter 2008): 57 kids from this trial and an identical 1997 pilot trial (33 jumpers, 24 stretchers, 47% of the first kids) had DXA bone scans 8 times over almost 8 years. Jumpers had 3.6% more hip bone mineral at 7 months and still 1.4% more after almost 8 years, after adjusting for age, height, weight and activity. The authors called it the first evidence that short, high-impact exercise in early childhood gives a lasting hip bone gain. They said it could lower fracture risk later in life, but only if the gain lasts into young adulthood.
events.citation: Gunter K, Baxter-Jones AD, Mirwald RL, Almstedt H, Fuchs RK, Durski S, Snow C. Impact exercise increases BMC during growth: an 8-year longitudinal study. Journal of Bone and Mineral Research. 2008;23(7):986-993. doi:10.1359/jbmr.071201. PMID 18072874. And: Fuchs RK, Bauer JJ, Snow CM. Jumping improves hip and lumbar spine bone mass in prepubescent children: a randomized controlled trial. J Bone Miner Res. 2001;16(1):148-156. doi:10.1359/jbmr.2001.16.1.148. PMID 11149479.
events.caution: This was jumping, not yoga. Stretching was the comparison group, and those kids gained less hip bone, so stretching alone did not build bone the same way. The study measured bone mineral, not broken bones, so it did not show fewer fractures. The gain after almost 8 years was small (1.4%), and only 47% of the first kids stayed for the long follow-up. The authors called the jumping safe for these healthy kids, who were trained step by step with adults watching. Kids with joint or bone problems should ask a doctor first.

events.topic: Older adults: balance, leg strength, flexibility, mood and sleep
events.title_line: University of Edinburgh · UK · 2019
events.headline: A review of 22 trials found yoga helped older adults' balance, leg strength, flexibility, mood and sleep.
events.meaning: Yoga is not only for the young. Older people in these trials got better balance, stronger legs and better sleep.
events.details: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 22 randomized controlled trials. People were older adults with an average age of 61 to 84, not chosen for any one disease (some were frail, inactive or had poor balance). Trials came from the USA (10), Australia (4), Taiwan (2), India (2), Brazil, Iran, UK and Portugal. Each trial had 18 to 410 people (average 77). The most common dose was 60 minutes, 2 days a week, and programs ran 4 to 28 weeks. Each result came from only some of the trials: balance from 7 trials (265 people), leg strength 7 trials (485 people), lower body flexibility 7 trials (431 people), depression 8 trials (450 people), sleep 4 trials (353 people). Compared with no exercise (wait-list, education booklet, social activities or usual care), yoga improved balance (effect size 0.70), leg strength (0.45), lower body flexibility (0.50), depression (0.64), sleep quality (0.65), mental health (0.60), physical health (0.61) and vitality (0.31). Compared with other exercise (tai chi, chair aerobics, walking, balance training, stretching and strengthening), yoga still gave better leg strength (0.49), better flexibility (0.28) and less depression (0.54), but not clearly better balance (0.32, not significant), mobility or walking speed. An effect size of about 0.5 is a medium change; 0.7 is medium to large.
events.citation: Sivaramakrishnan D, Fitzsimons C, Kelly P, Ludwig K, Mutrie N, Saunders DH, Baker G. The effects of yoga compared to active and inactive controls on physical function and health related quality of life in older adults: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act. 2019;16(1):33. doi:10.1186/s12966-019-0789-2. PMID 30953508.
events.caution: Better balance on a test is not the same as fewer falls. Balance results differed a lot between trials, mood and sleep were self-reported, and some trials had unclear risk of bias. Versus other exercise, yoga did not win for balance, mobility or walking speed. The large SAGE trial (University of Sydney, Lancet Healthy Longevity 2025;6:100749, 700 people aged 60+, mean age 67, 81% women) tested 80 one-hour, twice-weekly Iyengar-based classes over 12 months, run online because of COVID-19, against seated relaxation yoga. The active yoga group had MORE falls: 0.87 vs 0.64 falls per person per year (about 33% more), with no rise in falls that caused injury, although balance confidence and weekly exercise went up. The researchers said Iyengar yoga should not be recommended as a fall prevention strategy. Do not claim yoga prevents falls. Cochrane 2019 (Sherrington, 108 trials, 23,407 people) found balance and functional exercise lowered the rate of falls by 24%. Minor harms in the yoga trials: a groin muscle strain, a fall during class, some muscle pain.

events.topic: Longevity: the sit and rise from the floor test
events.title_line: CLINIMEX Exercise Medicine Clinic, Rio de Janeiro · Brazil · 2025
events.headline: Sit on the floor, stand up, no hands. Adults who could were far more often still alive 12 years later.
events.meaning: Rising from the floor needs strength, balance and flexibility, which asana trains. This simple skill is linked to a longer life.
events.details: Prospective cohort of 4,282 adults aged 46 to 75 (68% men), tested between 1998 and 2023 at an exercise medicine clinic in Rio de Janeiro. The sitting-rising test: sit down on the floor and stand back up. Sitting down scores up to 5 points and standing up scores up to 5, for 10 in total. Lose 1 point for each support used (hand or knee) and 0.5 for wobbling. People were followed for a median of 12.3 years, and 665 died of natural causes (15.5%). Death rate: 3.7% for a perfect score of 10, 11.1% for a score of 8, and 42.1% for scores of 0 to 4. After adjusting for age, sex, body mass index (BMI) and health conditions, the lowest scorers had 3.8 times the risk of natural death and 6.0 times the risk of heart-related death compared with perfect scorers. An earlier study by the same team (Brito et al., Eur J Prev Cardiol 2014;21(7):892-8; 2,002 adults aged 51 to 80, median 6.3 years) found each 1 point higher score was linked to 21% better survival.
events.citation: Araujo CGS, de Souza e Silva CG, Myers J, Laukkanen JA, Ramos PS, Ricardo DR. Sitting-rising test scores predict natural and cardiovascular causes of deaths in middle-aged and older men and women. Eur J Prev Cardiol. 2025 (print 2026;33(12):2170-2178). doi:10.1093/eurjpc/zwaf325. PMID 40569873.
events.caution: Observational: it shows a link, not that practice makes people live longer. This is not a yoga study. People were volunteers at one exercise clinic with no major limits for fitness testing, so results may not fit everyone. COVID and accidental or other outside-cause deaths were excluded. People with knee or hip problems, a joint replacement, or poor balance should not try the test alone: use a wall or a helper. Phrase slides around 'staying alive and well', not death counts.

events.topic: Chronic low back pain: yoga vs physical therapy
events.title_line: Boston Medical Center and Boston University · USA · 2017
events.headline: 12 weekly yoga classes helped long-term back pain about as much as 15 physical therapy visits did.
events.meaning: A gentle weekly class with asana, breathing and rest can be a real choice for long-term back pain, next to physical therapy.
events.details: Randomized trial of 320 adults with long-term low back pain, mostly low-income and racially diverse, average age about 46, at a Boston safety-net hospital and 7 community health centers. Three groups: 12 weekly 75-minute yoga classes (127 people), 15 physical therapy visits of 60 minutes (129 people), or a self-care book and newsletters (64 people). Each yoga class began with relaxation and meditation, yoga breathing and yoga philosophy, then asanas with chairs, straps and blocks, and ended with relaxation. 30 minutes of daily home practice was encouraged. After 12 weeks, the back function score (Roland Morris, a 23-point scale, lower is better) improved by 3.8 points with yoga, 3.5 with physical therapy and 2.5 with the book. The trial showed yoga was 'not worse' than physical therapy for both function and pain. 48% of the yoga group had a big gain in function (30% or more) vs 37% with physical therapy and 23% with the book. Used any pain medicine at 12 weeks: 54.8% yoga, 53.6% physical therapy, 75.4% book (about 21 percentage points fewer with yoga). Gains in the yoga and physical therapy groups lasted to 1 year. Side effects were mostly mild joint and back pain (9 yoga, 14 physical therapy, 1 book), with no real difference between yoga and physical therapy.
events.citation: Saper RB, Lemaster C, Delitto A, Sherman KJ, et al. Yoga, Physical Therapy, or Education for Chronic Low Back Pain: A Randomized Noninferiority Trial. Ann Intern Med. 2017;167(2):85-94. doi:10.7326/M16-2579. PMID 28631003. PMCID PMC6392183.
events.caution: On average, yoga was not clearly better than the book for either back function or pain, so say 'about as good as physical therapy', never 'better' or 'cures'. People knew which group they were in, and more people dropped out of the physical therapy group. The earlier Sherman 2011 trial (Group Health Research Institute, Seattle, 228 adults, Arch Intern Med 2011;171(22):2019-26) found yoga classes beat a self-care book but were no better than stretching classes. These were gentle, adapted classes with props, not a full Ashtanga series. New, severe back pain, or pain with leg weakness or numbness, should be checked by a doctor first.

events.title_line: AIIMS Rishikesh, India · Journal of Glaucoma · 2021
events.headline: Glaucoma patients who added daily yoga breathing to eye drops for 6 months lowered eye pressure about 2 points more.
events.meaning: Glaucoma can harm sight through high eye pressure. Daily pranayama helped lower it more, next to eye drops, never instead.
events.details: Randomized controlled trial at AIIMS Rishikesh, India. 90 people over age 40 with primary open-angle glaucoma (180 eyes), split into 2 groups of 45. Everyone kept using their eye drops. One group also did yogic pranayama (Anulom Vilom, alternate nostril breathing) plus belly (diaphragm) breathing, 30 minutes every day for 6 months: 4 weeks with a teacher, then at home. The other group used eye drops only (wait-list group). Eye pressure was checked at the start and after 1, 3 and 6 months. Breathing group: right eye 20.85 to 14.90 mmHg, left eye 20.30 to 14.25 mmHg, about 6 mmHg lower. The eye drops only group also went down: right eye 19.51 to 15.76, left eye 19.32 to 15.32, about 4 mmHg lower. So the breathing added about 2 mmHg of extra drop. The difference between groups was significant (P<0.001). 9 people (4 breathing, 5 control) missed some check-ups.
events.citation: Udenia H, Mittal S, Agrawal A, Singh A, Singh A, Mittal SK. Yogic Pranayama and Diaphragmatic Breathing: Adjunct Therapy for Intraocular Pressure in Patients With Primary Open-angle Glaucoma: A Randomized Controlled Trial. J Glaucoma. 2021;30(2):115-123. doi:10.1097/IJG.0000000000001697. PMID 33955942. Safety note: Commentary: The impact of yoga practice on glaucoma. Indian J Ophthalmol. 2023. PMID 37203028.
events.caution: The authors say clearly: breathing is an add-on, not a swap for eye drops or surgery. Never stop glaucoma medicine. Small study at one hospital, not blinded, eye pressure checked once a day only, no eye nerve scans or vision field tests. A 2023 commentary in the Indian Journal of Ophthalmology warns that breath holding may raise eye pressure, and head-down asana like headstand can double it. People with glaucoma should keep the breath smooth, skip long holds, and ask their eye doctor before inversions.

events.title_line: Mount Sinai, New York · 2015, and Sankara Nethralaya, Chennai · 2006
events.headline: Headstand doubled eye pressure. Downward dog raised it by about three quarters within 2 minutes.
events.meaning: Pressure went back to normal within 2 minutes of sitting up. Have glaucoma? Ask your eye doctor before any inversion.
events.details: Study 1, PLOS ONE 2015 (Jasien, Jonas, de Moraes, Ritch; New York Eye and Ear Infirmary of Mount Sinai). Design: one center, observational, no control treatment. 20 people: 10 with glaucoma (median age 62, 9 women) and 10 healthy (median age 36, 8 women). Each held 4 head-down asanas for 2 minutes. Eye pressure rose within 1 minute in every asana, in both groups. Downward dog (Adho Mukha Svanasana): glaucoma 17 to 28 mmHg, healthy 17 to 29 mmHg (average rise 72% and 79%). Standing forward bend (Uttanasana): 17 to 27 and 18 to 26 (61% and 48%). Plough (Halasana): 18 to 24 and 18 to 22 (33% and 28%). Legs up the wall (Viparita Karani): 17 to 21 in both (23% and 25%). Pressure went back to normal within 2 minutes of sitting up. Rise was about the same in glaucoma and healthy eyes. Study 2, Ophthalmology 2006 (Baskaran and team, Sankara Nethralaya, Chennai, India). Design: observational case series. 75 experienced practitioners from a yoga training institute (50 Indian, 25 Caucasian). In headstand (Sirsasana), eye pressure went up by about 15 mmHg right away and about 16 mmHg after 5 minutes: 2 times the starting level. It stayed high while they held the asana, in all age groups.
events.citation: Jasien JV, Jonas JB, de Moraes CG, Ritch R. Intraocular Pressure Rise in Subjects with and without Glaucoma during Four Common Yoga Positions. PLoS One. 2015;10(12):e0144505. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0144505. PMID 26698309. AND Baskaran M, Raman K, Ramani KK, Roy J, Vijaya L, Badrinath SS. Intraocular pressure changes and ocular biometry during Sirsasana (headstand posture) in yoga practitioners. Ophthalmology. 2006;113(8):1327-32. doi:10.1016/j.ophtha.2006.02.063. PMID 16806478.
events.caution: These are short spikes measured in small, non-randomized studies. Long-term harm in healthy eyes is not proven. The Glaucoma Research Foundation says the safest way for people with glaucoma is to avoid inversions, and to tell their yoga teacher so the practice can be changed. One case report (Indian Journal of Ophthalmology 2009, PubMed 19075418) describes a 55-year-old man on blood thinners, with a past lung clot, who lost vision in one eye from a blocked eye vein after headstand. Very relevant for Ashtanga, where downward dog comes in every sun salutation.

events.topic: Athletes and everyone: breath training review
events.title_line: ETH Zurich, Switzerland · 2012
events.headline: A review of 46 studies found breathing muscle training improved endurance in healthy people. Less fit people gained more.
events.meaning: You do not need to be an athlete. Less fit people and longer efforts showed bigger gains from breathing muscle training.
events.details: Systematic review and meta-analysis by ETH Zurich, published in Sports Medicine (2012). It pooled 46 original studies of healthy people who trained their breathing muscles with trainer devices. Sports studied included rowing, running, swimming and cycling. Less fit people improved more: about 6.0% more improvement for every 10 mL/kg/min lower fitness (VO2max). Longer efforts improved more: +0.4% for every extra minute of test time. 'How long can you last' tests at a steady pace showed about 16% more improvement than standard step-up tests, and interval step-up tests about 18.5% more. Race-style time trials showed no more change than standard step-up tests. The type of sport made no difference. A meta-analysis of 8 controlled trials confirmed a real improvement. Training both breathing in and breathing out may work best (+12.8% more than training breathing in only, but based on only 6 studies). A second review (University of British Columbia, 2013, 21 randomized trials in athletes) also found breathing muscle training improved sport performance, such as time trials and endurance time.
events.citation: Illi SK, Held U, Frank I, Spengler CM. Effect of respiratory muscle training on exercise performance in healthy individuals: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2012;42(8):707-724. doi:10.1007/BF03262290. PMID 22765281. Supporting: HajGhanbari B, Yamabayashi C, Buna TR, et al. Effects of respiratory muscle training on performance in athletes: a systematic review with meta-analyses. J Strength Cond Res. 2013;27(6):1643-1663. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e318269f73f. PMID 22836606.
events.caution: The 16% and 18.5% numbers compare types of tests. They do not mean everyone got 16% better. Race-style time trials showed smaller changes. Most of the pooled studies were small. Studies used breathing trainer devices, not yoga breathing (pranayama), so do not claim the same result for pranayama.

events.title_line: Paula Radcliffe · London Marathon · 2003
events.headline: Found to have asthma at about 14, Paula Radcliffe later ran a marathon world record that stood 16 years.
events.meaning: Asthma does not have to stop you. Work with your doctor, take the right medicine, and learn what sets it off.
events.details: As a teen, British runner Paula Radcliffe got dizzy after training and had trouble breathing. After she blacked out in training, her mum took her to a doctor. At about 14 she was found to have asthma. The doctor gave her inhalers and a peak flow meter, a tube that shows how hard you can blow out in one breath. She used it to check her lungs and know when to take more of her preventer medicine. He also told her that sport would make her lungs stronger. Oilseed rape in the fields near her new home was one of her main triggers, and she thinks more air pollution also played a part. Later her sports science team found which pollens set off her asthma, so she could avoid those training areas. On 13 April 2003 she ran the London Marathon in 2:15:25, a women's world record that stood for 16 years, until 2019. She won the London and New York marathons 3 times each. Her words: "You should control your asthma and not let it control you." She also says a marathon runner breathes in as much air in 3 hours as a person sitting still does in 2 days.
events.citation: World Athletics. Radcliffe: from elite athlete to clean air advocate (interview). worldathletics.org, 1 March 2019. Record broken by Brigid Kosgei, 2:14:04, Chicago, 13 Oct 2019 (Guinness World Records: "Brigid Kosgei smashes Paula Radcliffe's 16-year marathon record").
events.caution: One person's story, not a study. She used asthma medicine and her doctor's plan, not yoga. Exercise can set off asthma, so warm up slowly, follow your doctor's plan and keep your inhaler close.

events.topic: Athletes: credits yoga for a long career
events.title_line: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, NBA · 1969 to 1989
events.headline: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar says yoga helped him play 20 NBA seasons, until age 42, with few injuries.
events.meaning: He calls yoga one of the reasons, with martial arts and training. One person's story, but a strong example of steady practice.
events.details: On his website he writes: 'Yoga is one of the reasons that I was able to play professional basketball as long as I did with as few injuries as I had.' He says yoga has 'worked for me for over 45 years.' Before yoga he had lower back pain. He says his posture got better and 'my overall health improved significantly.' Sources differ on when he started: his site says 'since high school', while Wikipedia (citing a yoga expo article) says he began in 1976 in Los Angeles. He also credited martial arts training with Bruce Lee and a year-round fitness plan he began at age 26. Career facts (Britannica): born April 16, 1947; 20 NBA seasons, 1969-70 to 1988-89; retired in 1989 at age 42 with 38,387 points, the NBA all-time scoring record until LeBron James passed it in February 2023; record six-time MVP.
events.citation: Abdul-Jabbar K. 'Fit after 50: Staying Flexible With Yoga.' kareemabduljabbar.com. Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Kareem Abdul-Jabbar' biography, britannica.com/biography/Kareem-Abdul-Jabbar.
events.caution: One person's story, not a study: say 'he says yoga helped', never 'yoga made him' or 'yoga prevents injuries'. He also credits martial arts and conditioning, so do not present yoga as the only reason. Do not state 'since high school' as fact; sources disagree (high school vs 1976). Do not say he is the all-time top scorer today; LeBron James passed him in 2023. Do not name the hot-yoga brand or its founder (legal scandal), and leave out his political writing.

events.topic: Magical but true: breath and the immune system
events.title_line: Radboud University Medical Center · Nijmegen, Netherlands · 2014
events.headline: 12 men trained in breathing, cold and meditation. After a shot of dead germ parts, they felt 56% less sick.
events.meaning: Breathing may change how the body's defense system reacts. One small study in healthy young men found signs of this.
events.details: Design: randomized controlled trial, published in PNAS (May 2014). 24 healthy young men (median age 24 in the trained group, 22 in the control group, all aged 19 to 27). 12 men were trained for 10 days in the Wim Hof method: 4 days in Poland, then practice at home. The training had three parts: breathing (many fast deep breaths, then holding the breath), cold (ice water at 0 to 1°C, snow, hiking in the cold) and meditation. 12 men got no training. On the test day, the trained men did only the breathing exercises. Then all 24 got an injection of a tiny dose of dead bacteria parts (E. coli endotoxin, 2 ng per kg), which normally causes fever and flu-like feelings for a few hours. Results: before the injection, the trained men already had about 3 times more adrenaline in their blood (1.02 vs 0.35 nmol/L). 30 minutes into the breathing, it rose to 2.08. The authors wrote that mainly the breathing caused this rise. Their calming immune signal IL-10 was 194% higher. Inflammation signals were lower: TNF-alpha 53% lower, IL-6 57% lower, IL-8 51% lower. Flu-like symptoms (headache, nausea, shivering, muscle and back pain) were 56% lower at their worst. In the untrained group, temperature rose by about 1.9°C on average at its highest. In the trained group the rise was smaller and went back to normal sooner. During the breath holds, blood oxygen dipped to about 50% for around 10 seconds. Lead scientist Dr. Matthijs Kox: "The trained men produced more of the hormone epinephrine as a result of the techniques they had learned." Slide line idea: 12 men. 10 days of training. Inflammation signals about 50% lower. Flu-like symptoms 56% lower at their worst.
events.citation: Kox M, van Eijk LT, Zwaag J, van den Wildenberg J, Sweep FC, van der Hoeven JG, Pickkers P. Voluntary activation of the sympathetic nervous system and attenuation of the innate immune response in humans. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA. 2014;111(20):7379-7384. doi:10.1073/pnas.1322174111. PMID 24799686. Press release: Radboud University, "Modulating your own immune response" (ScienceDaily, 5 May 2014, https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2014/05/140505155210.htm).
events.caution: Small study: 24 healthy young men only, 12 per group. The 10-day training mixed breathing, ice cold water and meditation, so no one can say breath alone did it. The authors said their design cannot show which part of the breathing caused the effect. The researchers said it has not yet been tested in patients. Safety: the fast breathing plus breath hold method dropped blood oxygen to about 50% for short moments and can cause fainting. Never practice it in water, in a bath, while driving or while standing. Ask a doctor first if pregnant or living with heart problems, epilepsy or high blood pressure. This is not Ashtanga pranayama. Say so clearly on the slide.

events.topic: Magical but true: breath and body heat
events.title_line: Harvard Medical School team (Herbert Benson) · Himalayas, India · 1982
events.headline: 3 monks warmed their fingers and toes by up to 8.3°C during a breath and focus practice.
events.meaning: Real numbers, not legends: fingers and toes got warmer, but readings stayed between 22°C and 33°C, a normal range.
events.details: Design: small field study of 3 people (listed as case reports), published in Nature on 21 January 1982. Herbert Benson (Harvard Medical School) and colleagues from the USA and India tested 3 expert monks who practiced g Tum-mo (inner heat) meditation, a practice that uses breath and focus. Testing was done in February 1981 in the Himalayas of northern India. Results: finger and toe temperature rose by as much as 8.3°C. Skin at the navel and lower back rose about 1.9°C. Core body temperature (rectal) did not rise. A 2013 paper that looked back at this data notes the finger and toe readings stayed between 22°C and 33°C, which is a normal range. Follow-up study: National University of Singapore team (Kozhevnikov and colleagues, PLOS ONE, 2013) tested 10 expert meditators (7 women, ages 25 to 52, 6 to 32 years of practice) in remote mountain monasteries in Qinghai, China, above 4,200 m, in rooms near 0°C. Finger warming there came mostly from tensing the hands and pressing the fists into the hip crease, so the team measured armpit temperature instead. During the "Forceful Breath" practice with visualization, the 6 meditators who did it reached an average of 37.6°C and up to 38.3°C (slight fever zone). The biggest rise was 2.2°C. 11 Western yoga and martial arts practitioners in New Jersey, USA (10 women, ages 46 to 70, 7 to 30 years of practice) copied only the breathing, with no visualization. Their rises were smaller and stayed in the normal range. The team concluded the breathing makes the heat and the visualization helps keep it going longer. Slide line idea: 3 monks. One inner heat practice. Fingers and toes up to 8.3°C warmer. Published in Nature, 1982.
events.citation: Benson H, Lehmann JW, Malhotra MS, Goldman RF, Hopkins J, Epstein MD. Body temperature changes during the practice of g Tum-mo yoga. Nature. 1982;295(5846):234-236. doi:10.1038/295234a0. PMID 7035966. Follow-up: Kozhevnikov M, Elliott J, Shephard J, Gramann K. Neurocognitive and somatic components of temperature increases during g-Tummo meditation: legend and reality. PLoS One. 2013;8(3):e58244. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0058244 (open access: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0058244).
events.caution: Only 3 people, tested in 1981, never repeated in a large trial. Fingers and toes warmed but stayed in a normal range (22 to 33°C). The 2013 team found finger warming came mostly from tensing the hands, and notes that people using biofeedback or hypnosis (no meditation) have warmed their fingers by up to 11.7°C, so do not say the mind alone did it. Posts saying "17 degrees" are wrong: the top rise was 8.3°C (about 15°F). The 2013 team says steaming wet sheets do not prove higher body heat. Do not call it a superpower. Forceful breath holding is not for beginners, pregnant women, or people with heart problems or high blood pressure without a doctor's advice. For China-facing channels, describe the settings simply as "monks in the Himalayas of India" and "mountain monasteries in Qinghai, China", and do not name any political or religious leaders linked to the study.

events.topic: Magical but true: your nose makes its own gas
events.title_line: Karolinska Hospital and Institute · Stockholm, Sweden · 2002
events.headline: In 10 people, humming made nitric oxide gas in the nose 15 times higher than quiet breathing out.
events.meaning: Your nose makes a gas that helps blood vessels open. Nose breathing carries it to the lungs. Humming let out far more.
events.details: Design: small lab study by Eddie Weitzberg and Jon Lundberg at Karolinska in Stockholm, published in the American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine (15 July 2002). 10 healthy people. Scientists measured nitric oxide (NO) in air breathed out through the nose. NO is a gas made in the sinuses. It helps blood vessels open, and scientists think it may help keep germs down. They compared humming with quiet breathing out at the same air speed. Result: NO was 15 times higher during humming. Why: the scientists think the buzzing air moves air in and out of the sinuses. In a simple model of the nose and sinus, buzzing air made gas move between them much faster. Background 1 (Nature Medicine, 1995): Lundberg's team showed the sinuses make very high levels of NO, and suggested it may help keep the sinuses clean. Background 2, nose vs mouth (Acta Physiologica Scandinavica, 1996): in 6 of 8 healthy people, oxygen measured through the skin was 10% higher during nose breathing than during mouth breathing. The same paper says nose NO reaches the lungs when we breathe in, most of all through the nose. Link for Ashtanga: in every asana the breath goes in and out through the nose; humming is the sound of bhramari (bee breath). Slide line idea: Hum for one breath. In a study, the nose let out 15 times more nitric oxide.
events.citation: Weitzberg E, Lundberg JO. Humming greatly increases nasal nitric oxide. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2002;166(2):144-145. doi:10.1164/rccm.200202-138BC. PMID 12119224. Also: Lundberg JO, Farkas-Szallasi T, Weitzberg E, et al. High nitric oxide production in human paranasal sinuses. Nat Med. 1995;1(4):370-373. doi:10.1038/nm0495-370. PMID 7585069. Lundberg JO, Settergren G, Gelinder S, Lundberg JM, Alving K, Weitzberg E. Inhalation of nasally derived nitric oxide modulates pulmonary function in humans. Acta Physiol Scand. 1996;158(4):343-347. doi:10.1046/j.1365-201X.1996.557321000.x. PMID 8971255.
events.caution: Small studies: 10 people for humming, 8 people for nose vs mouth. They measured gas and oxygen levels, not illness. No study here shows humming prevents colds or sinus infections, so say "raised" or "let out more", never "protects" or "cures". The germ role of NO in the sinuses is an idea from the 1995 paper, not a proven effect. Bhramari itself was not tested; only plain humming was.

events.topic: Magical but true: the diaphragm helps the stomach
events.title_line: Medical University of Graz · Austria · 2012
events.headline: Four weeks of belly breathing cut the time acid spent in the food pipe almost in half.
events.meaning: Your breathing muscle also hugs the valve above your stomach. Training it helped people with acid reflux in a small trial.
events.details: Design: randomized controlled trial, published in the American Journal of Gastroenterology (March 2012, online December 2011). 19 adults with a milder type of acid reflux (non-erosive GERD, or a healed sore food pipe), without a large hernia or past surgery: 10 did a belly (diaphragm) breathing training program, 9 did not. Main test after 4 weeks. Results: time with acid in the food pipe (pH under 4) fell from 9.1% to 4.7% of the time measured in the training group; no change in the control group. Quality of life symptom score improved from 13.4 to 10.8 (lower is better); no change in the control group. All 19 were then invited to keep training. After 9 months, the 11 people who kept doing the breathing used much less acid medicine: from 98 to 25 mg per week, and their symptom score fell from 15.1 to 9.7. People who stopped training had no long-term effect. Why it works: the lower part of the diaphragm (the crura) wraps around the valve between the food pipe and the stomach, so training the breathing muscle helps that valve close. Supporting meta-analysis: Ningbo Medical Center Lihuili Hospital, Ningbo, China team (Annals of Palliative Medicine, 2020) pooled 7 studies (3 randomized trials) with 194 patients and 16 healthy volunteers: breathing exercises raised the pressure of this valve, and "to some extent" relieved symptoms. Slide line idea: Your diaphragm is not only for breathing. It also helps close the door above your stomach.
events.citation: Eherer AJ, Netolitzky F, Högenauer C, Puschnig G, Hinterleitner TA, Scheidl S, Kraxner W, Krejs GJ, Hoffmann KM. Positive effect of abdominal breathing exercise on gastroesophageal reflux disease: a randomized, controlled study. Am J Gastroenterol. 2012;107(3):372-378. doi:10.1038/ajg.2011.420. PMID 22146488. Supporting: Qiu K, Wang J, Chen B, Wang H, Ma C. The effect of breathing exercises on patients with GERD: a meta-analysis. Ann Palliat Med. 2020;9(2):405-413. doi:10.21037/apm.2020.02.35. PMID 32233626.
events.caution: Small trial (19 people, only 10 trained) with a 4 week main test; the 9 month group chose themselves whether to keep training, so that part has no fair comparison group. The meta-analysis pooled small studies and says only "to some extent". Never stop reflux medicine without a doctor. The popular line "the diaphragm massages your organs" was not measured here; the proven part is the diaphragm helping the stomach valve.
