Heartburn that lasts, or trouble swallowing, needs a doctor check.

Nothing is missing: 35 events and 15 quotes were returned. The input had duplicates (Craighead x2, Radcliffe x3, and Bajau twice), so there were 52 unique events to choose from. Evidence mix of the 35: 12 strong, 14 medium, 9 early. Honest flags for the slide writer:
(1) No study is on Ashtanga itself. Only Tulane mentions some Ashtanga asanas.
(2) Eight kept events are not yoga studies and must be labelled that way on the slide: Craighead and ETH (breathing devices), the swimming and jumping studies, sit-and-rise, Radcliffe (asthma medicine), Wim Hof (not Ashtanga pranayama), and humming (plain humming, not tested bhramari).
(3) Eyes: the only good evidence is a small drop in eye pressure in glaucoma. There is no proof yoga saves sight or helps short sight or dry eye. Put the inversion caution slide right after the glaucoma slide, because downward dog is in every sun salutation.
(4) The period pain yoga number rests on only 5 small trials.
(5) Older adults: better balance scores do not mean fewer falls. The SAGE 2025 trial found more falls with Iyengar yoga, so never claim yoga prevents falls.
(6) Quotes: 7 of the 15 are about breath, on purpose for this series. Mencius' 'heart' means heart-mind, not the organ, so do not pair it with a heart disease slide as if it were literal. Seneca's asthma quote fits well next to the asthma slides.
(7) Tummo slide: for China-facing channels, follow its caution and name no political or religious leaders.

all_events.title_line: University of Pavia and Santa Maria Nuova Hospital, Florence · Italy · 2001
all_events.headline: A rosary or a yoga mantra slowed breathing to about 6 breaths a minute and strengthened the blood pressure reflex.
all_events.meaning: Slow, steady breathing near 6 breaths a minute is free and simple. A prayer or a mantra can help set that pace.
all_events.details: 23 healthy adults (16 men, 7 women, average age 34) in Florence and Pavia, Italy. Researchers measured breathing, heart rhythm, blood pressure and brain blood flow in five states: quiet normal breathing, breathing to a set pace of 6 a minute, free talking, saying the Ave Maria (in Latin), and saying a yoga mantra. Normal quiet breathing was about 14 breaths a minute. The Ave Maria slowed it to 5.6 and the mantra to 5.7, close to one breath every 10 seconds. Breathing became much more even: the change from breath to breath fell from 37% during free talking to 8% with the Ave Maria and 6% with the mantra. The natural waves in heart rate and blood pressure got bigger and moved together. Baroreflex sensitivity (the body's fast blood pressure control) rose from 9.5 ms/mmHg during free talking to 11.5 with the Ave Maria and 12.3 with the mantra (P<0.05). The authors wrote that the rosary might be viewed as a health practice as well as a religious practice. Published in the BMJ, 22 December 2001.
all_events.citation: Bernardi L, Sleight P, Bandinelli G, Cencetti S, Fattorini L, Wdowczyc-Szulc J, Lagi A. Effect of rosary prayer and yoga mantras on autonomic cardiovascular rhythms: comparative study. BMJ. 2001;323(7327):1446-1449. doi:10.1136/bmj.323.7327.1446. PMID 11751348. PMCID PMC61046. Press release (BMJ Group, 20 Dec 2001): EurekAlert, https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/766123
all_events.caution: Small study: 23 healthy adults, measured during one lab session, not randomized. It shows body signals changed while people were reciting, not that any disease was prevented or that the effect lasts. Slow the breath gently; never strain or force it. Respectful framing only: present the rosary and the mantra as equals, never mock either.

all_events.topic: Heart rhythm: yoga and atrial fibrillation
all_events.title_line: University of Kansas Hospital · Kansas City, USA · 2013
all_events.headline: After 3 months of yoga, people with an irregular heartbeat had fewer symptom episodes on average: 2.1 instead of 3.8.
all_events.meaning: In this small study, people who added yoga to their normal heart care had fewer episodes and less anxiety and depression.
all_events.details: YOGA My Heart Study, one hospital, no separate control group. 52 adults with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (AF that comes and goes) enrolled and 49 finished (47% men, average age 61, AF for about 5 years, 78% on rhythm medicine). Each person was compared with themselves. First 3 months: normal life, no yoga. Next 3 months: Iyengar yoga with breathing, asana, meditation and relaxation, 60 minutes, at least twice a week. Results, yoga months vs the months before: symptom AF episodes fell from 3.8 to 2.1 (p<0.001). Other symptom heartbeat episodes fell from 2.9 to 1.4 (p<0.001). Silent AF episodes fell from 0.12 to 0.04 (p<0.001). Heart rate, top and bottom blood pressure all went down (p<0.001). Anxiety and depression scores dropped (p<0.001). Physical function, general health, vitality, social life and mental health scores went up. Published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology, March 2013.
all_events.citation: Lakkireddy D, Atkins D, Pillarisetti J, Ryschon K, Bommana S, Drisko J, Vanga S, Dawn B. Effect of yoga on arrhythmia burden, anxiety, depression, and quality of life in paroxysmal atrial fibrillation: the YOGA My Heart Study. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2013;61(11):1177-1182. doi:10.1016/j.jacc.2012.11.060. PMID 23375926. Enrolment, age, sex and medicine figures: ACC expert analysis, https://www.acc.org/latest-in-cardiology/articles/2014/07/18/17/24/yoga-for-paroxysmal-atrial-fibrillation-an-ancient-solution-to-an-emerging-problem. Lead doctor quote on blood thinners: Medical News Today, https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/221105
all_events.caution: Small study at one hospital (49 people), not randomized, no separate control group: people were compared with their own earlier 3 months, so it cannot prove yoga caused the change. Lead doctor Dhanunjaya Lakkireddy said yoga is strictly a supplement to medical care and patients should not stop their blood thinners. Ask your heart doctor before starting. Some news stories say 3 sessions a week of 45 minutes; the published paper says twice a week, 60 minutes, so use twice a week.

all_events.title_line: University of Connecticut · USA · 2019
all_events.headline: Across 49 trials, yoga lowered blood pressure. For high blood pressure, yoga with breathing and relaxation nearly doubled the drop.
all_events.meaning: The breath is not an extra. Yoga with breathing and relaxation gave the biggest blood pressure drop in these trials.
all_events.details: Meta-analysis (a study of studies) of 49 controlled trials with 56 yoga programs and 3,517 adults. Average age 49, average starting blood pressure 129/81. Average practice: about 5 sessions a week, 59 minutes each, for 13 weeks. Overall, yoga lowered top (systolic) blood pressure by 5.0 mmHg and bottom (diastolic) by 3.9 mmHg compared with control groups (P<0.001 for both). In the authors' best-case model for groups with high blood pressure practicing 3 times a week, yoga that included breathing techniques and meditation or relaxation lowered blood pressure by about 11/6 mmHg, compared with about 6/3 mmHg for yoga without them. Published in Mayo Clinic Proceedings, March 2019.
all_events.citation: Wu Y, Johnson BT, Acabchuk RL, Chen S, Lewis HK, Livingston J, Park CL, Pescatello LS. Yoga as antihypertensive lifestyle therapy: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Mayo Clin Proc. 2019;94(3):432-446. doi:10.1016/j.mayocp.2018.09.023. PMID 30792067.
all_events.caution: The 11/6 number comes from a statistical model of the best case, not from one single trial. Not every trial was randomized. Keep taking blood pressure medicine unless your doctor changes it. People with high blood pressure should breathe softly and avoid straining or hard breath holding. Ask a doctor first.

all_events.topic: Strong lungs, strong heart: breathing muscle training
all_events.title_line: University of Colorado Boulder · USA · 2021
all_events.headline: Just 30 hard breaths a day through a small device lowered top blood pressure by 9 points in 6 weeks.
all_events.meaning: Your breathing muscles can be trained like legs. Training them helped blood vessels and blood pressure in adults aged 50 to 79.
all_events.details: Double-blind randomized trial with a fake (sham) group. 36 adults aged 50 to 79 with top blood pressure of 120 or higher. They breathed in hard through a small hand-held device that pushes back, 30 breaths a day, 6 days a week, for 6 weeks (about 5 minutes a day). Real group (n=18) trained at 75% of their max breathing-in strength. Sham group (n=18) trained at only 15%, and nobody knew which group they were in. Real group: top blood pressure fell from 135 to 126 mmHg (P<0.01). Bottom number fell a little, from 79 to 77 mmHg (P=0.03). About 75% of the drop was still there 6 weeks after they stopped. 24-hour top blood pressure was also lower than in the sham group. Blood vessel function (flow-mediated dilation) improved about 45%. Sham group: no real change in blood pressure or blood vessel function. Artery stiffness did not change in either group. People completed about 95% of sessions. CU Boulder said the 9-point drop was generally bigger than what walking 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week gives, and about the same as some blood pressure drug plans. The method was first made in the 1980s to help very sick lung patients make their breathing muscles stronger. Published online in the Journal of the American Heart Association on 29 June 2021 (issue of July 2021).
all_events.citation: Craighead DH, Heinbockel TC, Freeberg KA, Rossman MJ, et al., Seals DR. Time-efficient inspiratory muscle strength training lowers blood pressure and improves endothelial function, NO bioavailability, and oxidative stress in midlife/older adults with above-normal blood pressure. J Am Heart Assoc. 2021;10(13):e020980. doi:10.1161/JAHA.121.020980. PMID 34184544. Trial NCT03266510. Press release: https://www.colorado.edu/today/2021/06/29/5-minute-breathing-workout-lowers-blood-pressure-much-exercise-drugs
all_events.caution: This used a resistance breathing device (inspiratory muscle training), not yoga pranayama, so do not say pranayama did this. Small study, 36 people, aged 50 to 79, only 6 weeks. Anyone with heart or lung disease, or on blood pressure medicine, should ask a doctor before strong breathing training.

all_events.title_line: Centre for Chronic Disease Control and 24 medical centers · India · 2020
all_events.headline: In 3,959 heart attack patients in India, gentle yoga with breathing helped people feel a little healthier.
all_events.meaning: Yoga may be an option for heart rehab when normal rehab clinics are missing. No problems happened during yoga sessions.
all_events.details: Randomized trial in 24 medical centers across India, run with the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine. 3,959 adults after a heart attack. 1,970 got Yoga-CaRe: 13 sessions over 12 weeks, about 75 minutes each, with gentle yoga movement, breath control, meditation and relaxation, led by trained yoga teachers, plus practice at home with booklets and videos. 1,989 got 3 sessions of health advice with a leaflet. Followed for a median of about 22 months. Self-rated health at 12 weeks: 77 vs 75.7 out of 100 (p=0.002). Return to normal daily activities from before the heart attack: score 88.3 vs 87.0 (p=0.039), a small gain. New major heart events: 6.7% vs 7.4%, not a significant difference. Taking medicines and quitting tobacco were the same in both groups. No adverse events were reported during the yoga sessions. Published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology, April 2020.
all_events.citation: Prabhakaran D, Chandrasekaran AM, Singh K, et al. Yoga-based cardiac rehabilitation after acute myocardial infarction: a randomized trial. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2020;75(13):1551-1561. doi:10.1016/j.jacc.2020.01.050. PMID 32241371. Full text: PMC7132532.
all_events.caution: The gains were small. The trial did not show that yoga prevents new heart events; it was too small to test that. Start only after your heart team says it is safe, and keep taking your heart medicines.

all_events.title_line: University of Copenhagen and UC Berkeley · Indonesia · 2018
all_events.headline: Bajau sea nomads have spleens about 50% bigger than their land neighbors, like a spare oxygen tank for diving.
all_events.meaning: Human bodies can adapt to breath holding in amazing ways, but this change took many generations, not one lifetime.
all_events.details: Melissa Ilardo and her team used ultrasound to measure the spleen in 59 Bajau people in Jaya Bakti village and 34 Saluan people, their neighbors who live on land and do not dive, on Sulawesi island, Indonesia. Bajau spleens were about 50% bigger. During a dive, the spleen squeezes and sends extra oxygen-carrying red blood cells into the blood. The team estimated the Bajau may get about 10% more of these cells in a dive than people without this change. Bajau who did not dive had spleens just as big as Bajau who did, so it seems to come from genes, not only training. The gene study found natural selection on a gene called PDE10A, linked to the bigger spleen. A second gene, BDKRB2, affects the diving reflex. Some Bajau dive deeper than 70 meters, spend up to 60% of their work day diving, and can be underwater up to 5 hours a day in total. Language studies suggest they have lived this sea life for more than 1,000 years.
all_events.citation: Ilardo MA, Moltke I, Korneliussen TS, et al., Nielsen R, Willerslev E. Physiological and Genetic Adaptations to Diving in Sea Nomads. Cell. 2018;173(3):569-580.e15. doi:10.1016/j.cell.2018.03.054. PMID 29677510. Press release: UC Berkeley News, 19 April 2018. Also NPR Goats and Soda, 24 April 2018.
all_events.caution: This change took many generations. Breath training will not make your spleen 50% bigger. Holding the breath in water can cause sudden blackout: never practice breath holds in water, and never alone.

all_events.title_line: Cochrane review, Chinese University of Hong Kong · 2016
all_events.headline: 15 trials, 1,048 people with asthma: yoga probably gave small gains in quality of life and symptoms.
all_events.meaning: A top medical review found small gains, not final proof. Use yoga next to asthma medicine, never instead of it.
all_events.details: Zuyao Yang and team pooled 15 randomized trials with 1,048 people. Most were adults with mild to moderate asthma. 8 trials were in India, 3 in the USA, 2 in the UK, 1 in Germany and 1 in Ethiopia. Programs lasted 2 weeks to 54 months, most up to 6 months. 5 trials used yoga breathing only. The other 10 mixed breathing, asana and meditation. Quality of life score went up 0.57 points more than in the other groups, on a 7 point scale (5 trials, 375 people). That is more than the 0.5 points doctors count as a real change. Symptoms got a little better (3 trials, 243 people). The lung blow test (FEV1) did not clearly change: plus 0.04 litres, not significant (7 trials, 340 people). No serious side effects were reported, but data was limited. The review rated the quality of life and symptom results moderate quality, and the lung test and safety results very low quality. The authors called the results early signs, not final proof.
all_events.citation: Yang ZY, Zhong HB, Mao C, Yuan JQ, Huang YF, Wu XY, Gao YM, Tang JL. Yoga for asthma. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2016;(4):CD010346. doi:10.1002/14651858.CD010346.pub2. PMID 27115477.
all_events.caution: Yoga did not clearly change the lung test number (FEV1). In 2 trials that used a fake breathing method for comparison, quality of life did not clearly improve. Keep taking asthma medicine as your doctor says, and keep your inhaler near your mat.

all_events.title_line: University of Duisburg-Essen, Germany · 2019
all_events.headline: In 11 trials with 586 COPD patients, yoga helped people walk farther and blow out more air.
all_events.meaning: Sick lungs can work a little better with practice. Gains showed up only in breathing-focused yoga (pranayama), not programs with asana.
all_events.details: Holger Cramer and team pooled 11 randomized trials with 586 people with COPD, a long-term lung disease that makes breathing hard. Compared with no treatment, people who did yoga walked about 25.5 meters farther in a 6 minute walk test. Lung function (FEV1, the air you can blow out in 1 second) rose by about 4 percentage points of the expected value for their body (3.95%). Quality of life also improved (3.81 points on the COPD Assessment Test), but that result was less solid and did not hold up when weaker studies were checked. The surprise: the gains showed up only in breathing-focused yoga, not in programs that included asana. Few trials reported on side effects, so the authors say safety needs more study. An earlier review (Liu and team, Shandong University, China, 2014, 5 trials, 233 patients) found FEV1 up about 124 mL and walking up about 39 meters.
all_events.citation: Cramer H, Haller H, Klose P, Ward L, Chung VC, Lauche R. The risks and benefits of yoga for patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Clinical Rehabilitation. 2019;33(12):1847-1862. doi:10.1177/0269215519860551. PMID 31353959. Also: Liu XC, Pan L, Hu Q, Dong WP, Yan JH, Dong L. Effects of yoga training in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Thorac Dis. 2014;6(6):795-802. doi:10.3978/j.issn.2072-1439.2014.06.05. PMID 24977005.
all_events.caution: Yoga breathing is an add-on to lung rehab and medicine, not a swap. People with COPD should ask their doctor before strong or fast breathing practices.

all_events.topic: Breathing muscles: heart and blood pressure
all_events.title_line: University of Colorado Boulder · USA · 2021
all_events.headline: 30 hard breaths a day through a small device lowered top blood pressure 9 points in 6 weeks.
all_events.meaning: Training your breathing muscles can help blood pressure and blood vessels. A few minutes a day made a real difference.
all_events.details: Daniel Craighead, Douglas Seals and team at the University of Colorado Boulder ran a double-blind randomized trial. 38 adults aged 50 to 79 joined. All had top (systolic) blood pressure of 120 or higher. 36 finished. 18 people breathed in hard through a small hand device. The resistance went up from 55% to 75% of their strongest breath in by week 3. They did 30 breaths a day, 6 days a week, for 6 weeks, about 5 minutes each time. 18 others used a fake easy setting (15%). High resistance group: top blood pressure went from 135 to 126, bottom from 79 to 77. Fake group: top went from 134 to 131, too small to count as a real change, and bottom stayed at 81. About 75% of the drop was still there 6 weeks after they stopped. Blood vessel function (how well the arm artery opens) was about 45% better. The fake group did not improve on this. The high resistance group did about 94% of their sessions. The university said a 9 point drop is usually more than walking 30 minutes a day, 5 days a week, gives. Craighead said it can be done in 5 minutes at home while you watch TV.
all_events.citation: Craighead DH, Heinbockel TC, Freeberg KA, Rossman MJ, et al., Bailey EF, Seals DR. Time-Efficient Inspiratory Muscle Strength Training Lowers Blood Pressure and Improves Endothelial Function, NO Bioavailability, and Oxidative Stress in Midlife/Older Adults With Above-Normal Blood Pressure. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2021;10(13):e020980. doi:10.1161/JAHA.121.020980. PMID 34184544. Trial NCT03266510.
all_events.caution: This used a special breathing trainer device, not yoga breathing. Small study of 36 people aged 50 to 79, not tested in kids. Anyone with high blood pressure should keep their medicine and ask their doctor before starting.

all_events.title_line: Paula Radcliffe · London Marathon · 2003
all_events.headline: Found to have asthma at 14, Paula Radcliffe ran a marathon world record that stood for 16 years.
all_events.meaning: Asthma does not have to stop you. Work with your doctor, take the right medicine, and learn what sets it off.
all_events.details: As a teen, British runner Paula Radcliffe got dizzy after training and had trouble breathing. After she blacked out in training, her mum took her to a doctor. At about 14 she was found to have asthma. The doctor gave her inhalers and a peak flow meter, a tube that shows how hard you can blow out in one breath. She used it to check her lungs and know when to take more of her preventer medicine. He also told her that sport would make her lungs stronger. Oilseed rape in the fields near her new home was one of her main triggers, and she thinks more air pollution also played a part. Later her sports science team found which pollens set off her asthma, so she could avoid those training areas. On 13 April 2003 she ran the London Marathon in 2:15:25, a women's world record that stood for 16 years, until 2019. She won the London and New York marathons 3 times each. Her words: "You should control your asthma and not let it control you." She also says a marathon runner breathes in as much air in 3 hours as a person sitting still does in 2 days.
all_events.citation: World Athletics. Radcliffe: from elite athlete to clean air advocate (interview). worldathletics.org, 1 March 2019. Record broken by Brigid Kosgei, 2:14:04, Chicago, 13 Oct 2019 (Guinness World Records: "Brigid Kosgei smashes Paula Radcliffe's 16-year marathon record").
all_events.caution: One person's story, not a study. She used asthma medicine and her doctor's plan, not yoga. Exercise can set off asthma, so warm up slowly, follow your doctor's plan and keep your inhaler close.

all_events.title_line: Stanford University · 2023
all_events.headline: Five minutes a day of breathing with long, slow out-breaths lifted good mood more than meditation did.
all_events.meaning: You do not need an hour. Five minutes of long, slow out-breaths is a free tool you can carry everywhere.
all_events.details: Randomized controlled trial run fully at home (remote) in 2020 by Stanford School of Medicine (Spiegel and Huberman labs). 108 adults aged 18 and over, 5 minutes per day, for 28 days. Four groups: cyclic sighing (30 people: breathe in through the nose, then a second short breath in to fill the lungs, then a slow full breath out through the mouth), box breathing (21), fast breathing with breath holds (33), and mindfulness meditation (24). Average daily rise in good mood (PANAS scale, 10 to 50): 1.91 points for the three breathing groups together vs 1.22 for meditation (cyclic sighing 1.89, fast breathing 1.97, box breathing 1.84). In the study's main model, cyclic sighing was the best at lifting mood over the month, and the gain grew the more days people practiced. Only cyclic sighing lowered resting breathing rate clearly more than meditation, measured each day by a wrist strap. People whose breathing rate dropped the most also had the biggest mood lift (r = -0.24). All four groups felt less anxious and less bad mood right after each session. The authors think, but did not test, that part of the calming effect may travel through the vagus nerve, which links brain, heart and lungs.
all_events.caution: One small trial, mostly healthy adults, done at home, so nobody checked how people really practiced. Meditation lowered anxiety and bad mood just as well; breathing only won on good mood. Heart rate variability, resting heart rate, sleep and long-term anxiety did not change. One author (Huberman) advises WHOOP, the company that made the wrist strap. The study left out people with heart disease, glaucoma, seizures, pregnancy, bipolar disorder, psychosis or serious mental illness, so those people should ask a doctor first, especially before fast breathing with breath holds.
all_events.citation: Balban MY, Neri E, Kogon MM, Weed L, Nouriani B, Jo B, Holl G, Zeitzer JM, Spiegel D, Huberman AD. Brief structured respiration practices enhance mood and reduce physiological arousal. Cell Rep Med. 2023;4(1):100895. doi:10.1016/j.xcrm.2022.100895. PMID 36630953. PMCID PMC9873947. Trial NCT05304000.

all_events.title_line: Boston University School of Medicine · 2010
all_events.headline: Yoga beat walking for mood and worry. Brain scans linked better mood to a calming brain chemical, GABA.
all_events.meaning: Same effort as walking, yet the asana group felt happier and less anxious. Asana may calm the mind in its own way.
all_events.details: Randomized trial of healthy adults aged 18 to 45. Iyengar yoga or walking matched for the same energy use, 60 minutes, 3 times a week, for 12 weeks. 34 people finished: 19 yoga, 15 walking. The yoga group reported a bigger lift in mood and a bigger drop in anxiety than the walkers. Brain scans (MR spectroscopy) found that higher GABA in the thalamus went together with better mood and less anxiety. GABA is the brain's main 'slow down' chemical, and many anti-anxiety medicines work on it. Earlier pilot from the same team (2007): after one 60-minute yoga session, 8 experienced practitioners had a 27% rise in brain GABA; 11 people who read for 60 minutes had no change.
all_events.caution: Small studies (34 people, and only 8 yoga people in the 27% pilot). People were healthy, not patients with anxiety or depression. The class was Iyengar yoga, not Ashtanga. In the 2010 trial the GABA rise right after class was only 'nearly significant' (p = 0.09); the clear finding was the link between GABA and mood. Yoga helps next to medical care for anxiety, not instead of it.
all_events.citation: Streeter CC, Whitfield TH, Owen L, Rein T, Karri SK, Yakhkind A, Perlmutter R, Prescot A, Renshaw PF, Ciraulo DA, Jensen JE. Effects of yoga versus walking on mood, anxiety, and brain GABA levels: a randomized controlled MRS study. J Altern Complement Med. 2010;16(11):1145-1152. doi:10.1089/acm.2010.0007. PMID 20722471. PMCID PMC3111147. Pilot: Streeter CC et al. Yoga Asana sessions increase brain GABA levels: a pilot study. J Altern Complement Med. 2007;13(4):419-426. doi:10.1089/acm.2007.6338. PMID 17532734.

all_events.title_line: University of Pennsylvania · 2017
all_events.headline: Still depressed on medicine, people added a breathing practice. In 8 weeks, they improved much more than people who waited.
all_events.meaning: A breathing practice may help next to medicine, even when medicine alone has not helped enough. Never stop medicine on your own.
all_events.details: Randomized pilot trial at the University of Pennsylvania, USA, October 2014 to December 2015. 25 adults (ages 18 to 67, 18 of them women) with major depression who were still depressed after at least 8 weeks on a steady dose of antidepressants. 13 were put in the Sudarshan Kriya Yoga (SKY) group. SKY is a set of rhythm breathing exercises. Week 1 had 6 sessions of 3.5 hours: SKY plus yoga asana, sitting meditation and stress lessons. Weeks 2 to 8 had one 1.5 hour group session each week, plus 20 to 25 minutes of SKY at home every day. 12 people waited (waitlist) and got the program later. Everyone kept the same medicine dose. After 8 weeks, the Hamilton depression score (checked by raters who did not know the groups) dropped 9.77 points with SKY vs rose 0.50 on the waitlist. The Beck depression score dropped 17.23 vs 1.75. The Beck anxiety score dropped 5.44 vs 0.25. 46% of the SKY group (6 of 13) had their depression score cut by more than half, vs 8% on the waitlist, and 31% reached remission, vs 8%. With so few people, these two gaps were not statistically clear. 10 of 13 in the SKY group finished every part. No side effects were reported.
all_events.caution: Small pilot (25 people). The raters were blinded, but the people knew if they were doing SKY, and there was no active comparison group, so extra attention and group support may explain part of the gain. Never stop or change antidepressants without your doctor. People with bipolar disorder, epilepsy or pregnancy were left out of this study. SKY includes fast breathing, so learn it from a trained teacher, and ask a doctor first if you have one of these conditions or a heart problem.
all_events.citation: Sharma A, Barrett MS, Cucchiara AJ, Gooneratne NS, Thase ME. A breathing-based meditation intervention for patients with major depressive disorder following inadequate response to antidepressants: a randomized pilot study. J Clin Psychiatry. 2017;78(1):e59-e63. doi:10.4088/JCP.16m10819. PMID 27898207. PMCID PMC5272872. Trial NCT02616549.

all_events.title_line: University of South Australia & UNSW Sydney · 2020
all_events.headline: 13 trials, 632 people with mental health conditions: moving yoga lowered depression symptoms. More sessions each week, bigger drops.
all_events.meaning: Showing up often may matter. Trials with more yoga sessions each week saw bigger drops in depression symptoms.
all_events.details: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (search up to 14 May 2019). Authors from University of South Australia, UNSW Sydney, Federal University of Santa Maria (Brazil), King's College London and University of Manchester. Only physically active yoga counted: at least 50% of each session spent moving, holding asana and flowing through sequences. The review found 19 trials with 1,080 adults who had a diagnosed mental disorder (depression, PTSD, schizophrenia, anxiety, alcohol dependence, bipolar disorder). 13 trials (632 people) were pooled: yoga lowered depressive symptoms more than waitlist, usual care or attention control (standardized mean difference 0.41, p < 0.001). Trials with more yoga sessions per week showed bigger drops (beta = -0.44, p < 0.01). UNSW's Simon Rosenbaum: 'The more sessions per week people engaged in, the greater the benefit was.'
all_events.caution: The pooled trials were small, about 49 people each on average. The link between more sessions and bigger drops compares trials, so it is not proof for each person. The researchers say more data is needed on yoga type, intensity and breathing. Yoga here was compared with waitlist, usual care or attention control, so keep any doctor-led treatment going.
all_events.citation: Brinsley J, Schuch F, Lederman O, Girard D, Smout M, Immink MA, Stubbs B, Firth J, Davison K, Rosenbaum S. Effects of yoga on depressive symptoms in people with mental disorders: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Sports Med. 2021;55(17):992-1000 (online 18 May 2020). doi:10.1136/bjsports-2019-101242. PMID 32423912.

all_events.title_line: University of Sussex & University of Oxford, UK · 2023
all_events.headline: 12 trials, 785 adults: people who practiced breathing had less stress than others. More trials found less anxiety and depression.
all_events.meaning: Slow breathing, as in pranayama, now has support from trials: it helped lower stress by a small to medium amount.
all_events.details: Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, searched up to February 2022 (1,325 records found at first). Stress: 12 trials, 785 adults (417 did breathwork, 368 were in control groups). People who did breathwork had lower stress than control groups (effect size g = -0.35, small to medium, p = 0.0009). Anxiety: 20 trials, g = -0.32. Depressive symptoms: 18 trials, g = -0.40. Of the 12 stress trials, 10 taught slow breathing and 2 taught fast breathing. 6 were in people with a physical illness, 5 in people without illness, and 1 in a mental health group. The clear drop in stress showed up with slow breathing and in people without illness. For fast breathing and for patient groups the result was not clear, because there were few studies. Estimated minimum practice time ranged from 80 to 5,625 minutes in total. Half of the stress trials were self-help, with no live teacher. Four stress trials (six in all) checked for harm. None reported adverse events or lasting bad effects caused by the breathing.
all_events.caution: Most trials were small and had a moderate risk of bias. The authors say breathwork 'may be' effective and warn against hype. For people with a physical or mental illness the stress result was not clear, so the authors say it is too early to recommend it as treatment there. Only adults were studied. In one fast-breathing depression study, a small group felt hot flushes, shortness of breath or sweating. They chose to keep going and no one quit because of it. Fast breathing (like kapalabhati) needs advice first in pregnancy, epilepsy, heart problems or panic attacks. If you feel dizzy, stop and breathe normally.
all_events.citation: Fincham GW, Strauss C, Montero-Marin J, Cavanagh K. Effect of breathwork on stress and mental health: a meta-analysis of randomised-controlled trials. Sci Rep. 2023;13(1):432. doi:10.1038/s41598-022-27247-y. PMID 36624160. PMCID PMC9828383.

all_events.title_line: Beijing University of Chinese Medicine · China · 2025
all_events.headline: In a big review, adults with insomnia who did yoga reported almost 2 more hours of sleep each night.
all_events.meaning: Yoga may be a low cost, gentle way to help sleep. Use it next to your doctor's advice, not instead of it.
all_events.details: Scientists pooled 22 randomized trials with 1,348 adults with insomnia. They compared 13 treatments, and 7 of them were exercise: yoga, tai chi, walking or jogging, strength training, and other types. Programs lasted 4 to 26 weeks. Compared with people given usual care or lifestyle advice, people who did yoga wrote down in sleep diaries about 111 more minutes of sleep a night. The share of time in bed spent asleep went up by about 15.6 points. Time awake in the night dropped by about 56 minutes, and people fell asleep about 29 minutes faster. Tai chi and walking or jogging also helped. The authors found yoga, tai chi and walking or jogging worked better than the other exercises. Published online 15 July 2025 in BMJ Evidence-Based Medicine (print issue 2026).
all_events.caution: The yoga numbers come from sleep diaries people filled in, not sleep lab machines. The authors rated certainty as moderate for total sleep time and low for the other yoga results. Only 4 of the 22 trials were rated low risk of bias, and the authors say bigger, better trials are needed. Long insomnia can have medical causes, so people should also see a doctor. Say yoga 'helped', never that it fixes insomnia.
all_events.citation: Bu ZJ, Liu FS, Shahjalal M, et al. Effects of various exercise interventions in insomnia patients: a systematic review and network meta-analysis. BMJ Evid Based Med. 2026;31(2):102-113. Published online 15 July 2025. doi:10.1136/bmjebm-2024-113512. PMID 40664502.

all_events.title_line: Swami Vivekananda Yoga Research Foundation · Bangalore, India · 2005
all_events.headline: Older adults who did yoga for 6 months said they slept about 1 hour more and felt more rested.
all_events.meaning: Sleep often breaks up more with age. A yoga program of asana, breathing and relaxation helped older people say they slept better.
all_events.details: From 120 people living in a home for older adults, 69 were sorted by age and then split by chance into 3 groups: yoga (asana, relaxation, breath control and talks on yoga philosophy), an Ayurveda herbal mix, or a wait list with nothing new. Each person rated their own sleep for one week at the start, at 3 months and at 6 months. After 6 months, the yoga group said they fell asleep about 10 minutes faster, slept about 60 minutes more in total, and felt more rested in the morning. The herbal group and the wait list group showed no real change. Published in the Indian Journal of Medical Research, May 2005.
all_events.caution: Sleep was self-rated, not measured with machines. Small study, about 23 people per group, in one home. The yoga program also had philosophy talks, so we cannot say which part helped most. Older students with heart, blood pressure or balance problems should start gently and check with a doctor first.
all_events.citation: Manjunath NK, Telles S. Influence of Yoga and Ayurveda on self-rated sleep in a geriatric population. Indian J Med Res. 2005;121(5):683-690. PMID 15937373.

all_events.title_line: Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard · Boston, USA · 2005
all_events.headline: Long-time meditators had thicker brain areas for focus and feeling the body, with the biggest focus-area gap in older people.
all_events.meaning: Daily sitting was linked to thicker focus areas. It might help slow normal brain thinning with age, but more proof is needed.
all_events.details: Sara Lazar's team used MRI scans on 20 people with about 9 years of Insight meditation practice (on average they sat about 40 minutes once a day and reported about 6 hours a week) and 15 people with no meditation or yoga experience. Average age was about 37 to 38. Meditators had thicker brain areas linked to attention and sensing the body, including the right prefrontal cortex (planning and focus) and the right anterior insula (feeling inside the body, like the breath). In that prefrontal area, the non-meditators showed the usual thinning with age, but the meditators did not. So the authors suggest meditation might slow normal brain thinning with age. Breath fact: during meditation, people with more lifetime hours of practice slowed their breathing more. In two areas (a visual area and the insula), people whose breathing slowed more had thicker brain tissue. Published in NeuroReport, November 2005. The authors called it the first brain-structure evidence linked to meditation practice.
all_events.caution: Small snapshot study of 35 people: it shows a link, not proof that meditation caused the change. People who choose to meditate may be different in other ways. A later 8-week study from the same Harvard group (Hölzel 2011, 16 new meditators vs 17 wait-list people, Psychiatry Research: Neuroimaging, doi:10.1016/j.pscychresns.2010.08.006) found denser grey matter in the left hippocampus, a memory area, which supports the idea. Meditation is not a treatment for memory loss.
all_events.citation: Lazar SW, Kerr CE, Wasserman RH, et al. Meditation experience is associated with increased cortical thickness. NeuroReport. 2005;16(17):1893-1897. doi:10.1097/01.wnr.0000186598.66243.19. PMID 16272874. PMCID PMC1361002.

all_events.title_line: Northwestern University · Chicago, USA · 2016
all_events.headline: People recognized pictures better when the picture came on an in-breath through the nose. Mouth breathing lost this.
all_events.meaning: Ashtanga asks for steady nose breathing. This study found brain waves in memory and feeling areas move with the nose breath.
all_events.details: Christina Zelano and Jay Gottfried's team first studied 7 people with epilepsy who already had electrodes in their brains, placed to find where seizures started before surgery. Brain waves in the smell area, the amygdala (fear and feeling) and the hippocampus (memory) moved in time with the breath. They were strongest on the in-breath. In 3 of these patients, the waves faded when they breathed through the mouth. Then healthy young adults, ages 18 to 30, did two lab tests. Fear test (70 people): they spotted fearful faces faster when the face came on a nose in-breath than on an out-breath. Surprised faces showed no change. Memory test (42 people): they saw pictures of objects, then later picked out the ones they had seen before. They were more accurate when the test picture came on a nose in-breath. The breath phase when they first saw the picture did not matter. These effects were not seen in the groups who breathed through the mouth. Published in the Journal of Neuroscience, 7 December 2016.
all_events.caution: Small lab study. The memory test was a short picture test, not long-term memory, and the healthy people were only 18 to 30 years old. It does not show nose breathing treats memory problems or anxiety. The patients were not named; keep it that way. People with a blocked nose should not force nose breathing.
all_events.citation: Zelano C, Jiang H, Zhou G, Arora N, Schuele S, Rosenow J, Gottfried JA. Nasal Respiration Entrains Human Limbic Oscillations and Modulates Cognitive Function. J Neurosci. 2016;36(49):12448-12467. doi:10.1523/JNEUROSCI.2586-16.2016. PMID 27927961. PMCID PMC5148230. Press release: https://news.northwestern.edu/stories/2016/12/rhythm-of-breathing-affects-memory-and-fear

all_events.title_line: University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign · USA · 2014
all_events.headline: After 8 weeks of yoga, older adults got faster and sharper on memory and task-switching tests than a stretching group.
all_events.meaning: Starting in your 60s still counts. Three 1-hour classes a week for 8 weeks helped thinking skills, not only the body.
all_events.details: Neha Gothe, Arthur Kramer and Edward McAuley split 118 adults (average age 62) by chance: 61 to Hatha yoga and 57 to a stretching and strengthening class. Both groups had 1-hour classes 3 times a week for 8 weeks. Yoga classes included asana, sun salutations, alternate nostril breathing and meditation. 108 people finished, and both groups came to about 81% of classes. The yoga group got faster at switching between tasks and more accurate on working memory tests (the 2-back test and part of a memory span test) than the stretching group. Published online July 2014, in the September 2014 issue of the Journal of Gerontology: Medical Sciences.
all_events.caution: The gains were small to medium and were tested right after the 8 weeks, so we do not know how long they last. One memory score (total recall) did not change enough to count. Most people in the study were white women who did not exercise much before. It was not a dementia study. Older beginners should modify asana; people with glaucoma or high blood pressure should skip headstand and other upside-down asana unless their doctor says it is OK.
all_events.citation: Gothe NP, Kramer AF, McAuley E. The effects of an 8-week Hatha yoga intervention on executive function in older adults. J Gerontol A Biol Sci Med Sci. 2014;69(9):1109-1116. doi:10.1093/gerona/glu095. PMID 25024234. PMCID PMC4202261.

all_events.title_line: University of Rochester (YOCAS trial) · USA · 2013
all_events.headline: In a 410-person trial, 4 weeks of gentle yoga helped cancer survivors sleep better and use fewer sleeping pills.
all_events.meaning: Gentle breathing, soft asana and rest helped adults sleep better after cancer treatment. Older survivors said it helped too.
all_events.details: 410 adult cancer survivors who slept badly, 2 to 24 months after surgery, chemo or radiation (96% women, average age 54, 75% breast cancer). Run by 9 community cancer programs in 12 US cities, 2007 to 2010. Chosen by chance: 206 got yoga plus usual care, 204 got usual care only. Yoga: 2 classes a week, 75 minutes each, for 4 weeks, in small groups of about 12. Each class had pranayama (breathing), 16 gentle Hatha and restorative asanas, and meditation. Results (people with full data, 168 yoga and 153 usual care): the sleep problem score (lower is better) dropped 1.96 points (9.2 to 7.2) with yoga vs 1.07 points with usual care. Sleeping pill use went down 21% per week in the yoga group but went up 5% per week in the usual care group. The yoga group also had fewer daytime problems and spent less time awake at night (measured by a wrist sleep tracker). 90% said yoga helped their sleep. A 2024 look at the same trial (177 people from the yoga group with full data): those aged 60 and over had less tiredness too, like the younger ones, and 88.5% of the older group said yoga helped their sleep.
all_events.caution: Most people were women with breast cancer, and 22% did not give full data. Sleep got better in both groups; the extra gain from yoga was under 1 point on the score. The yoga was gentle Hatha and restorative, not a full Ashtanga series. It helped sleep and tiredness only; it does not treat the cancer itself. Anyone still in treatment should ask their cancer doctor first.
all_events.citation: Mustian KM, Sprod LK, Janelsins M, Peppone LJ, Palesh OG, Chandwani K, Reddy PS, Melnik MK, Heckler C, Morrow GR. Multicenter, randomized controlled trial of yoga for sleep quality among cancer survivors. J Clin Oncol. 2013;31(26):3233-3241. doi:10.1200/JCO.2012.43.7707. PMID 23940231. PMCID PMC3757292. Follow up (yoga group only): Arana-Chicas E, Lin PJ, Gada U, et al. The effect of YOCAS yoga on cancer-related fatigue and quality of life in older (60+) vs. younger (59 and under) cancer survivors: secondary analysis of a nationwide, multicenter, phase 3 randomized controlled trial. J Geriatr Oncol. 2024;15(8):102076. doi:10.1016/j.jgo.2024.102076. PMID 39368335.

all_events.topic: Cancer patients and survivors: fatigue and inflammation
all_events.title_line: Ohio State University · USA · 2014
all_events.headline: Breast cancer survivors who did yoga had 57% less tiredness and less inflammation than a no-yoga group, months later.
all_events.meaning: The benefit was bigger 3 months after classes ended. The lead scientist thinks the breathing and meditation parts were really important.
all_events.details: 200 breast cancer survivors, ages 27 to 76, stage 0 to 3A, who had finished surgery or radiation 2 months to 3 years before. 100 women did Hatha yoga classes 2 times a week, 90 minutes each, for 12 weeks, and were asked to practice at home too. 100 women were on a wait list and did no yoga during the study. Right after the 12 weeks: the yoga group had a 12% higher vitality (energy) score. 3 months after classes ended (6 months into the study): fatigue was 57% lower than in the no-yoga group. When their blood cells were tested in the lab, they made 13 to 20% less of 3 inflammation proteins (IL-6, TNF-alpha, IL-1 beta). Women who practiced more often got bigger changes. The yoga group also slept better. Lead scientist Janice Kiecolt-Glaser: "We think the breathing and meditation components were really important in terms of some of the changes we were seeing."
all_events.caution: Right after the 12 weeks, the drop in fatigue was not yet clear by statistics. The big difference showed 3 months later. Depression scores did not differ between groups. The no-yoga group got no other class, so part of the effect may come from attention and group support (the authors say this). Tiredness was self-reported. The 57% and 13 to 20% numbers come from the Ohio State news release. This helped side effects and wellbeing only, not the cancer itself.
all_events.citation: Kiecolt-Glaser JK, Bennett JM, Andridge R, et al. Yoga's impact on inflammation, mood, and fatigue in breast cancer survivors: a randomized controlled trial. J Clin Oncol. 2014;32(10):1040-1049. doi:10.1200/JCO.2013.51.8860. PMID 24470004. PMCID PMC3965259. Numbers from Ohio State News release, 26 January 2014.

all_events.topic: Cancer patients and survivors: yoga vs stretching during radiation
all_events.title_line: MD Anderson Cancer Center with VYASA (Bengaluru, India) · Houston, USA · 2014
all_events.headline: During breast cancer radiation, yoga helped women's daily physical function more than stretching did, even 6 months later.
all_events.meaning: A yoga class mixing asanas, breathing, relaxation and meditation gave extra help beyond stretching. The study cannot say which part mattered most.
all_events.details: 163 women with breast cancer (stage 0 to 3), about to start 6 weeks of radiation, were split by chance into 3 groups: yoga (53 women), simple stretching (56) or waiting list (54). Yoga and stretching classes were up to 3 times a week, 60 minutes each. The yoga class had a warm up linked to the breath, gentle asanas (bending forward, back and sideways, cobra, crocodile, and a supported half shoulder stand), deep relaxation lying down, alternate nostril breathing (pranayama) and meditation. Teachers were trained by VYASA in Bengaluru, India. Stretching was taught by MD Anderson physiotherapists. Results: at 1, 3 and 6 months after radiation, the yoga group reported better physical functioning (daily tasks like walking, lifting and climbing stairs) than BOTH the stretching group and the waiting group. By the end of radiation, yoga and stretching both lowered fatigue more than waiting. In saliva tests, the yoga group's stress hormone (cortisol) fell more steeply from morning to night at the end of radiation and 1 month later, a daily rhythm scientists link to better health.
all_events.caution: Yoga did not beat stretching or waiting for mood, depression or sleep scores. This was one hospital, and results come from the women who finished the tests. The class used a supported half shoulder stand: after breast surgery, with a chest port, arm swelling (lymphedema), cancer in the bones or low blood counts, inversions and strong asanas should be changed or skipped. Ask the cancer team first.
all_events.citation: Chandwani KD, Perkins G, Nagendra HR, et al. Randomized, controlled trial of yoga in women with breast cancer undergoing radiotherapy. J Clin Oncol. 2014;32(10):1058-1065. doi:10.1200/JCO.2012.48.2752. PMID 24590636. PMCID PMC3965260.

all_events.topic: Breast cancer: big Cochrane review of yoga trials
all_events.title_line: Cochrane Review, University of Duisburg-Essen · Germany · 2017
all_events.headline: A review of 24 trials with 2,166 women with breast cancer found yoga lowered tiredness and sleep trouble.
all_events.meaning: Cochrane reviews are among medicine's most careful checks. Yoga eased side effects like tiredness as an add-on to cancer care.
all_events.details: Holger Cramer and team at the University of Duisburg-Essen in Germany pooled 24 randomized trials with 2,166 women with breast cancer, during or after treatment. Yoga vs no yoga, short term (moderate quality evidence): better quality of life (10 studies, 675 women), less fatigue (11 studies, 883 women) and less sleep trouble (6 studies, 657 women). These trials reported no serious side effects. Yoga vs talk or education programs, short term (moderate quality evidence): less depression (4 studies, 226 women), less anxiety (3 studies, 195 women) and less fatigue (2 studies, 106 women). Yoga vs other exercise: no clear difference (very low quality evidence, 3 studies, 233 women). A newer 2025 Cochrane review from the University of Cologne (21 trials, 2,041 adults with any type of cancer) found yoga AFTER treatment probably lowers fatigue in the short term (5 studies, 602 people, moderate certainty).
all_events.caution: Compared with no yoga, it did not clearly lower depression or anxiety (low and very low quality evidence), and no clear effect was found in the medium term (only 2 studies, 146 women). For yoga DURING cancer treatment, the 2025 review says the evidence is very uncertain. Yoga helped side effects only. It is an add-on to medical care, not a replacement.
all_events.citation: Cramer H, Lauche R, Klose P, Lange S, Langhorst J, Dobos GJ. Yoga for improving health-related quality of life, mental health and cancer-related symptoms in women diagnosed with breast cancer. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2017;1:CD010802. doi:10.1002/14651858.CD010802.pub2. PMID 28045199. Also: Messer S, Oeser A, Wagner C, et al. Yoga for fatigue in people with cancer. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2025;5:CD015520. doi:10.1002/14651858.CD015520. PMID 40421669.

all_events.topic: Cancer patients and survivors: official doctor guideline
all_events.title_line: Society for Integrative Oncology and ASCO · USA and Canada · 2023
all_events.headline: Top cancer doctor groups (ASCO and SIO) say yoga may be offered for anxiety and depression in people with cancer.
all_events.meaning: Yoga is now part of official cancer care advice. Doctors can offer it next to medical treatment, not instead of it.
all_events.details: In 2023, an expert panel from the Society for Integrative Oncology and the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO), with Linda Carlson of the University of Calgary as lead author, looked at 110 studies: 30 systematic reviews and 80 randomized trials, published from 1990 to 2023. Yoga was recommended for anxiety during and after cancer treatment, and for depression during and after treatment. The best proof was for people with breast cancer: yoga during treatment got a moderate strength recommendation. For other cancers, the advice for yoga was weak, because there were fewer good studies. In 2024, a second ASCO and SIO guideline on cancer tiredness (fatigue) looked at 113 randomized trials from 2013 to 2023. It said yoga may be recommended for fatigue after treatment ends. It also said doctors should not recommend antidepressants or wakefulness drugs to manage cancer fatigue.
all_events.caution: The guideline puts yoga next to medical care, never in place of it. Most of the proof comes from women with breast cancer, and many trials had no active comparison group. The panels rated the proof for these therapies as low to moderate quality. Teachers should adapt practice to each body and follow the advice of the patient's doctor.
all_events.citation: Carlson LE, Ismaila N, Addington EL, et al. Integrative Oncology Care of Symptoms of Anxiety and Depression in Adults With Cancer: Society for Integrative Oncology-ASCO Guideline. J Clin Oncol. 2023;41(28):4562-4591. doi:10.1200/JCO.23.00857. PMID 37582238. Also: Bower JE, Lacchetti C, Alici Y, et al. Management of Fatigue in Adult Survivors of Cancer: ASCO-Society for Integrative Oncology Guideline Update. J Clin Oncol. 2024;42(20):2456-2487. doi:10.1200/JCO.24.00541. PMID 38754041.

all_events.title_line: National Taiwan University Hospital and partners · Taiwan · 2024
all_events.headline: After 8 weeks of yoga, period pain was 2.75 points lower (out of 10) than with no exercise.
all_events.meaning: A steady practice may make painful periods easier. Slow, calm relaxation work helped the most, and fewer people quit it.
all_events.details: A big review (network meta-analysis) joined 29 randomized trials with 1,808 people with period pain. Almost all were young women and teen girls aged 15 to 26. Pain was scored on a 0 to 10 line. Each exercise group was compared with a group that did no exercise program (nothing or usual care). After 8 weeks, yoga lowered pain by 2.75 points more than no exercise. After 4 weeks the yoga drop was 1.63 points, and that result only just counted as real. Other movement also helped after 8 weeks: aerobic exercise 2.77 points, strength training 3.17 points, mixed exercise 3.67 points, and relaxation exercise 3.87 points, the biggest drop. Relaxation exercise meant slow muscle relaxation or belly self massage, and it was the only type where fewer people quit than in the no exercise group. The yoga number came from 5 small trials (about 197 people in yoga groups) from Iran, Japan, Turkey and Egypt. Yoga programs ran from 8 minutes a day to 60 minutes three times a week. Authors' conclusion: all exercise types lowered period pain after 8 weeks.
all_events.caution: The yoga result rests on only 5 small trials, so the number is not exact. The review did not grade evidence quality, and more than half of the trials had some risk of bias. Almost everyone studied was 15 to 26, so we know less about older women. A 2019 Cochrane review (Armour et al., 12 trials, 854 women; DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD004142.pub4) agrees: exercise such as yoga, stretching or aerobics, about 45 to 60 minutes, 3 times a week or more, may cut period pain by about 25 points out of 100 compared with no exercise, but it rated the evidence low quality. Very strong pain, or pain that gets worse over the years, should be checked by a doctor (it can be a sign of endometriosis).
all_events.citation: Tsai IC, Hsu CW, Chang CH, Lei WT, Tseng PT, Chang KV. Comparative Effectiveness of Different Exercises for Reducing Pain Intensity in Primary Dysmenorrhea: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Sports Medicine - Open, 2024;10:63. DOI: 10.1186/s40798-024-00718-4

all_events.topic: Women: PMS (mood and body changes before a period)
all_events.title_line: University of Birmingham and Loughborough University · UK · 2020
all_events.headline: A review of 15 trials with 717 women found regular exercise, yoga included, eased PMS symptoms.
all_events.meaning: The tired, cranky, teary days before a period may get lighter when you move your body regularly.
all_events.details: UK researchers joined 15 randomized trials with 717 women (average ages 17 to 34). Programs were about 3 times a week, 30 to 60 minutes each, for 8 to 12 weeks. Types: aerobic exercise, yoga (2 trials), Pilates, water aerobics, stretching and resistance work. Each was compared with a group that did no exercise. Total PMS score (7 trials, 265 women) dropped a lot (standardized difference -1.08). Mood symptoms (8 trials, 427 women) -1.67. Body symptoms (7 trials, 397 women) -1.62. Behavior symptoms (only 2 trials, 92 women) -1.94. Strength of evidence was rated moderate. Authors' words: exercise may be an effective treatment for PMS, but some uncertainty remains.
all_events.caution: Most trials were small, 12 of 15 came from Iran, and 13 of 15 had a high risk of bias. Results varied a lot between trials. Only 2 trials tested yoga, so say 'exercise like yoga'. Very low mood, anger or hopeless feelings before periods (PMDD) need a doctor, not only practice.
all_events.citation: Pearce E, Jolly K, Jones LL, Matthewman G, Zanganeh M, Daley A. Exercise for premenstrual syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. BJGP Open, 2020;4(3). DOI: 10.3399/bjgpopen20X101032

all_events.title_line: University of Duisburg-Essen and University of Technology Sydney · Germany and Australia · 2018
all_events.headline: In 13 trials with 1,306 women, yoga eased menopause symptoms, from low mood to hot flashes and aches.
all_events.meaning: Midlife women may have fewer menopause symptoms, like low mood and hot flashes, with regular yoga, much like other exercise.
all_events.details: Review and meta-analysis of 13 randomized trials with 1,306 women (studies searched up to February 2017). Compared with no treatment, yoga lowered total menopause symptoms by a large amount (effect size -1.05), mood and mind symptoms (-0.75), body symptoms like aches (-0.65), hot flashes and night sweats (-0.76), and urinary and vaginal symptoms (-0.53). Compared with other exercise, yoga was about the same for most symptoms. The only extra benefit was a small to medium drop in hot flashes (-0.45). No serious side effects were reported. Authors: yoga seems effective and safe for menopause symptoms, with effects like other exercise.
all_events.caution: The results were less sure in trials where the people scoring the results knew who did yoga, or where many women dropped out. The Menopause Society (2023 position statement) does not recommend yoga as a treatment for hot flashes, saying the evidence is too weak. Say 'helped symptoms and mood', not 'stops hot flashes'. Yoga is not a replacement for seeing a doctor.
all_events.citation: Cramer H, Peng W, Lauche R. Yoga for menopausal symptoms: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Maturitas, 2018;109:13-25. DOI: 10.1016/j.maturitas.2017.12.005 (PubMed 29452777)

all_events.topic: Women: menopause hot flashes and sleep
all_events.title_line: MsFLASH research network, Group Health Research Institute Seattle and partners · USA · 2014
all_events.headline: 12 weeks of yoga did not cut hot flashes more than usual life, but women had less trouble sleeping.
all_events.meaning: Honest science: yoga is not a fix for hot flashes, but a little less trouble sleeping in midlife still matters.
all_events.details: Randomized trial at 3 US sites (Indianapolis, Oakland, Seattle). 249 women aged 40 to 62 (average 54) with about 7 to 8 hot flashes a day: 107 did yoga, 142 kept their usual activity. The yoga group did 12 weekly 90-minute classes: breathing work (with 'cooling' breaths), 11 to 13 asanas (restorative, inversions, side bends, twists, forward bends) and Yoga Nidra deep relaxation, plus 20 minutes at home on other days. 95% finished. Hot flashes fell 35% with yoga and 27% with usual activity, a gap too small to be sure it was real (0.3 fewer a day, p = 0.119). Insomnia score fell 4.4 points with yoga vs 3.1 without (p = 0.007), a modest gain. Sleep quality and mood scores leaned better too, but did not pass the study's bar for proof. New side effects were similar in both groups (33.7% vs 39.3%), none serious.
all_events.caution: A large, well-run trial found yoga did not lower hot flashes more than usual activity. Use it for a modest drop in insomnia, not for hot flash or deep sleep claims. The yoga was a gentle Viniyoga-style program, not Ashtanga.
all_events.citation: Newton KM, Reed SD, Guthrie KA, et al. Efficacy of yoga for vasomotor symptoms: a randomized controlled trial. Menopause. 2014;21(4):339-346. DOI: 10.1097/GME.0b013e31829e4baa (PMID 24045673)

all_events.title_line: Jersey Shore University Medical Center · Neptune, New Jersey, USA · 2015
all_events.headline: 25 women, 35 to 37 weeks pregnant, did 26 asanas while doctors watched. Baby heart rates stayed normal.
all_events.meaning: In healthy pregnancies, one session of these asanas showed no warning signs for mother or baby, even late on.
all_events.details: 25 healthy pregnant women at 35 to 37 weeks each did one private session of 26 asanas with a certified yoga teacher. 10 did yoga often, 8 knew some yoga, 7 had never done yoga. Doctors checked the mother's vital signs, blood oxygen and womb contractions, and watched the baby's heart rate the whole time, in every asana. The set included asanas many people thought were risky in late pregnancy: Adho Mukha Svanasana (downward dog), Ananda Balasana (happy baby), Balasana (child) and Savasana lying on the back. All readings stayed normal in every woman and every asana. Before and after the session, the mother's heart rate, temperature and blood oxygen and the baby's heart rate did not change. No falls or injuries across 650 asanas in total. In the next 24 hours, no woman reported less baby movement, contractions, fluid leak or bleeding. Published in Obstetrics and Gynecology.
all_events.caution: Small study, one session only, healthy pregnancies only, no comparison group. The lead doctor called it preliminary. Headstands and lying on the belly were left out. ACOG advice: modified yoga is fine, avoid hot yoga, avoid lying on the back or staying still for long periods, avoid activities with high fall risk. A 2016 US randomized trial (Babbar et al., 52 women at 28 to 36 weeks, DOI 10.1016/j.ajog.2015.12.032) also found no change in blood flow to the baby after a first yoga class. Always check with a doctor or midwife first.
all_events.citation: Polis RL, Gussman D, Kuo YH. Yoga in Pregnancy: An Examination of Maternal and Fetal Responses to 26 Yoga Postures. Obstetrics & Gynecology, 2015;126(6):1237-1241. DOI: 10.1097/AOG.0000000000001137 (PubMed 26551176)

all_events.title_line: Tulane University · New Orleans, USA · 2018
all_events.headline: Worried third graders who did breathing, relaxation and kid asanas, some from Ashtanga, before school felt better in 8 weeks.
all_events.meaning: A short practice before class may help a worried child. Ten 40-minute sessions showed a change in this small study.
all_events.details: Randomized controlled trial at one public elementary school in New Orleans. 52 third graders who screened positive for anxiety symptoms on the SCARED test were randomized one by one: 20 got yoga, 32 got usual care (counseling and other activities with the school social worker). Yoga group: 10 small-group sessions, 40 minutes each (400 minutes total), in an empty classroom before the school day, over 8 weeks. One group of 10 kids did it in the fall and another 10 in the spring (the study ran Oct 2016 to Feb 2017). Sessions used the Yoga Ed curriculum: breathing exercises, guided relaxation, and 'several Vinyasa and Ashtanga' asanas made for third graders, led by an experienced children's yoga teacher. Kids filled in the PedsQL quality of life survey about their own feelings. Result: the emotional score went UP 18.27 points in the yoga group and DOWN 0.86 points in the usual care group (p = 0.009). In the adjusted model: +14.17 emotional score (p = 0.001) and +7.43 psychosocial score (p = 0.01). Physical, social and school scores did not change in a statistically significant way. Teachers who got 2 training sessions said they used yoga in class more often (from 1.28 to 2.39 times a week, p = 0.03).
all_events.caution: Small study at one school: only 20 kids in the yoga group, and the two yoga groups did it at different times of the year. Breathing, relaxation and asanas were mixed together, so we cannot say which part helped, or that Ashtanga itself was the key. Kids rated their own feelings; it measured quality of life scores, not a medical diagnosis. Physical, social and school scores did not improve significantly. The teacher numbers were self-reported and not part of the randomized test. Yoga can add to, but not replace, help from a counselor or doctor for an anxious child.
all_events.citation: Bazzano AN, Anderson CE, Hylton C, Gustat J. Effect of mindfulness and yoga on quality of life for elementary school students and teachers: results of a randomized controlled school-based study. Psychology Research and Behavior Management. 2018;11:81-89. doi:10.2147/PRBM.S157503. PMID 29695937. Tulane press release, Apr 2018: https://news.tulane.edu/pr/school-based-yoga-can-help-children-better-manage-stress-and-anxiety

all_events.title_line: University of Illinois · USA · 2014
all_events.headline: Kids who played hard after school for 9 months got fitter hearts and lungs and a little sharper focus.
all_events.meaning: Active play on most school days helped kids' brains, not just bodies. They got a little better at focus and switching tasks.
all_events.details: FITKids randomized controlled trial. 221 children aged 7 to 9 were randomly put in a 9-month after-school activity program or a wait list. The program ran 2 hours after school on 150 of the 170 school days, at a recreation center on the University of Illinois campus. Each session had activity stations and skill games, with at least 70 minutes of moderate to hard activity (checked with heart rate monitors). Kids came to about 81% of sessions. Average heart rate was about 137 beats per minute, and kids took about 4,246 steps per session. Results vs wait list: heart and lung fitness (VO2max) rose 1.3 mL/kg/min more; ignoring distractions (inhibition) improved 3.2% more; switching between tasks (cognitive flexibility) improved 4.8% more. Brain wave tests (P3) showed bigger attention signals only in the active group. Kids who came more often improved a bit more (r = 0.22 and 0.24, small links). Published in Pediatrics.
all_events.caution: This was active games and play, not yoga. The gains were real but small (about 3 to 5 percent), and the focus gain only just passed the line for chance. The program was 2 hours a day on most school days, much more than most kids get, so do not promise the same result from one class a week. This is one study at one site.
all_events.citation: Hillman CH, Pontifex MB, Castelli DM, Khan NA, Raine LB, Scudder MR, Drollette ES, Moore RD, Wu CT, Kamijo K. Effects of the FITKids randomized controlled trial on executive control and brain function. Pediatrics. 2014;134(4):e1063-e1071. doi:10.1542/peds.2013-3219. PMID 25266425.

all_events.title_line: Cochrane Review, Beggs and team · Hobart, Australia · 2013
all_events.headline: Kids with stable asthma who swam 6 to 12 weeks got fitter, and their lungs worked a little better.
all_events.meaning: Stable asthma need not stop kids moving. Swimming did not make asthma worse. Keep medicine and ask the doctor first.
all_events.details: Cochrane systematic review led by a team at Royal Hobart Hospital, Australia. It pooled 8 randomized trials with 262 children and teens aged 5 to 18 with stable asthma, mild to severe. In 7 trials, kids swam 30 to 90 minutes, 2 to 3 times a week, for 6 to 12 weeks. In 1 trial they swam 30 minutes, 6 times a week. Control groups had usual care (7 trials) or played golf (1 trial). Fitness: VO2max (how much oxygen the body can use) rose by 9.67 mL/kg/min compared with usual care (2 trials, 32 kids). Other fitness tests rose by a similar amount (4 trials, 74 kids). Lungs: FEV1 (how much air you can blow out in 1 second) rose by about 8 points of percent predicted (8.07), which the authors called a small gain. Based on limited data, swimming did not harm asthma control or cause more attacks, and few asthma problems were reported. The authors rated the fitness gain as high-strength evidence and the lung gain as moderate-strength evidence, and said swimming was well tolerated.
all_events.caution: Swimming did NOT improve asthma control, asthma attacks, quality of life or steroid use. The trials were small, and 3 of them had many kids drop out. The review could not tell if swimming is better than other sports. Pool chlorine was unknown in 4 trials, so ask a doctor about indoor chlorinated pools. Kids must keep taking their asthma medicine and carry their reliever inhaler. A separate review of breathing exercises and yoga/pranayama for asthmatic kids (Das 2019, 10 trials, 466 kids aged 6 to 14) found mixed results and said it cannot yet be a standard treatment, so we cannot claim pranayama alone helps asthma.
all_events.citation: Beggs S, Foong YC, Le HC, Noor D, Wood-Baker R, Walters JA. Swimming training for asthma in children and adolescents aged 18 years and under. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2013;(4):CD009607. doi:10.1002/14651858.CD009607.pub2. PMID 23633375. Related: Das RR, Sankar J, Kabra SK. Role of breathing exercises and yoga/pranayama in childhood asthma: a systematic review. Curr Pediatr Rev. 2019;15(3):175-183. doi:10.2174/1573396315666190121122452. PMID 30663571.

all_events.title_line: Paula Radcliffe · London Marathon · 2003
all_events.headline: Diagnosed with asthma at about 14 after blacking out in training, Paula Radcliffe later set a marathon world record.
all_events.meaning: With a doctor's care and the right medicine, a child with asthma can still run and even become a champion.
all_events.details: Paula Radcliffe, British distance runner, born 17 December 1973. At about age 14, a year after her family moved from Cheshire to Bedfordshire, she felt dizzy and had trouble breathing after training. Then she blacked out in training, and her mother took her to the doctor. She was found to have exercise-induced asthma. Triggers: pollen (oilseed rape fields were one of her main triggers), pollution and dust. Her doctor told her to use inhalers and gave her a peak flow meter (a tube that measures how much air you can blow out fast and hard in one breath). She says it 'made a huge difference' and that she still uses it. She told The Irish Times she warmed up gently over about 45 minutes before races. On 13 April 2003, at the London Marathon, she ran 2:15:25, a women's world record that stood for 16 years, until 2019. She also won London (2002, 2003, 2005), New York (2004, 2007, 2008) and the 2005 World Championship marathon in Helsinki.
all_events.caution: One person's story, not a study. Her success came with asthma medicine, a doctor's care and a careful warm-up, not yoga. Do not say yoga helped her. Breath practice is an add-on, never a swap for a child's inhaler.
all_events.citation: Humphreys G (for WHO). 'Radcliffe: from elite athlete to clean air advocate.' World Athletics, 1 March 2019. Also: Winter G. 'Exercise can take your breath away, for all the wrong reasons.' The Irish Times, 13 Dec 2016 (https://www.irishtimes.com/life-and-style/health-family/fitness/exercise-can-take-your-breath-away-for-all-the-wrong-reasons-1.2889394); 'Athletics legend Paula Radcliffe joins fight for clean air.' BreatheLife2030 (WHO/UNEP campaign), 6 Nov 2018 (https://breathelife2030.org/news/athletics-legend-paula-radcliffe-joins-fight-clean-air/).

all_events.title_line: Oregon State University · USA · 2001 and 2008
all_events.headline: Kids who jumped 7 months at school still had more hip bone than kids who stretched, almost 8 years later.
all_events.meaning: Childhood is a key time to build bone. Stretching did not build bone like jumping did, so let kids jump too.
all_events.details: Randomized trial (Fuchs 2001, Corvallis, Oregon): 89 children aged 5.9 to 9.8, before puberty, split into a jumping group (45) and a stretching group (44). Both groups trained at school 3 days a week for 7 months. Jumpers built up to 100 two-footed jumps off a 61 cm (24 inch) box each session; landings hit about 8 times body weight. The stretching group did no-impact stretching on the same schedule. After 7 months, jumpers gained 4.5% more bone mineral at the hip (femoral neck) and 3.1% more at the lower spine than the stretching group. Height, weight and body fat grew the same in both groups. Follow-up (Gunter 2008): 57 kids from this trial and an identical 1997 pilot trial (33 jumpers, 24 stretchers, 47% of the first kids) had DXA bone scans 8 times over almost 8 years. Jumpers had 3.6% more hip bone mineral at 7 months and still 1.4% more after almost 8 years, after adjusting for age, height, weight and activity. The authors called it the first evidence that short, high-impact exercise in early childhood gives a lasting hip bone gain. They said it could lower fracture risk later in life, but only if the gain lasts into young adulthood.
all_events.caution: This was jumping, not yoga. Stretching was the comparison group, and those kids gained less hip bone, so stretching alone did not build bone the same way. The study measured bone mineral, not broken bones, so it did not show fewer fractures. The gain after almost 8 years was small (1.4%), and only 47% of the first kids stayed for the long follow-up. The authors called the jumping safe for these healthy kids, who were trained step by step with adults watching. Kids with joint or bone problems should ask a doctor first.
all_events.citation: Gunter K, Baxter-Jones AD, Mirwald RL, Almstedt H, Fuchs RK, Durski S, Snow C. Impact exercise increases BMC during growth: an 8-year longitudinal study. Journal of Bone and Mineral Research. 2008;23(7):986-993. doi:10.1359/jbmr.071201. PMID 18072874. And: Fuchs RK, Bauer JJ, Snow CM. Jumping improves hip and lumbar spine bone mass in prepubescent children: a randomized controlled trial. J Bone Miner Res. 2001;16(1):148-156. doi:10.1359/jbmr.2001.16.1.148. PMID 11149479.

all_events.topic: Chronic low back pain: yoga vs physical therapy
all_events.title_line: Boston Medical Center and Boston University · USA · 2017
all_events.headline: 12 weekly yoga classes helped long-term back pain about as much as 15 physical therapy visits did.
all_events.meaning: A gentle weekly class with asana, breathing and rest can be a real choice for long-term back pain, next to physical therapy.
all_events.details: Randomized trial of 320 adults with long-term low back pain, mostly low-income and racially diverse, average age about 46, at a Boston safety-net hospital and 7 community health centers. Three groups: 12 weekly 75-minute yoga classes (127 people), 15 physical therapy visits of 60 minutes (129 people), or a self-care book and newsletters (64 people). Each yoga class began with relaxation and meditation, yoga breathing and yoga philosophy, then asanas with chairs, straps and blocks, and ended with relaxation. 30 minutes of daily home practice was encouraged. After 12 weeks, the back function score (Roland Morris, a 23-point scale, lower is better) improved by 3.8 points with yoga, 3.5 with physical therapy and 2.5 with the book. The trial showed yoga was 'not worse' than physical therapy for both function and pain. 48% of the yoga group had a big gain in function (30% or more) vs 37% with physical therapy and 23% with the book. Used any pain medicine at 12 weeks: 54.8% yoga, 53.6% physical therapy, 75.4% book (about 21 percentage points fewer with yoga). Gains in the yoga and physical therapy groups lasted to 1 year. Side effects were mostly mild joint and back pain (9 yoga, 14 physical therapy, 1 book), with no real difference between yoga and physical therapy.
all_events.caution: On average, yoga was not clearly better than the book for either back function or pain, so say 'about as good as physical therapy', never 'better' or 'cures'. People knew which group they were in, and more people dropped out of the physical therapy group. The earlier Sherman 2011 trial (Group Health Research Institute, Seattle, 228 adults, Arch Intern Med 2011;171(22):2019-26) found yoga classes beat a self-care book but were no better than stretching classes. These were gentle, adapted classes with props, not a full Ashtanga series. New, severe back pain, or pain with leg weakness or numbness, should be checked by a doctor first.
all_events.citation: Saper RB, Lemaster C, Delitto A, Sherman KJ, et al. Yoga, Physical Therapy, or Education for Chronic Low Back Pain: A Randomized Noninferiority Trial. Ann Intern Med. 2017;167(2):85-94. doi:10.7326/M16-2579. PMID 28631003. PMCID PMC6392183.

all_events.topic: Older adults: balance, leg strength, flexibility, mood and sleep
all_events.title_line: University of Edinburgh · UK · 2019
all_events.headline: A review of 22 trials found yoga helped older adults' balance, leg strength, flexibility, mood and sleep.
all_events.meaning: Yoga is not only for the young. Older people in these trials got better balance, stronger legs and better sleep.
all_events.details: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 22 randomized controlled trials. People were older adults with an average age of 61 to 84, not chosen for any one disease (some were frail, inactive or had poor balance). Trials came from the USA (10), Australia (4), Taiwan (2), India (2), Brazil, Iran, UK and Portugal. Each trial had 18 to 410 people (average 77). The most common dose was 60 minutes, 2 days a week, and programs ran 4 to 28 weeks. Each result came from only some of the trials: balance from 7 trials (265 people), leg strength 7 trials (485 people), lower body flexibility 7 trials (431 people), depression 8 trials (450 people), sleep 4 trials (353 people). Compared with no exercise (wait-list, education booklet, social activities or usual care), yoga improved balance (effect size 0.70), leg strength (0.45), lower body flexibility (0.50), depression (0.64), sleep quality (0.65), mental health (0.60), physical health (0.61) and vitality (0.31). Compared with other exercise (tai chi, chair aerobics, walking, balance training, stretching and strengthening), yoga still gave better leg strength (0.49), better flexibility (0.28) and less depression (0.54), but not clearly better balance (0.32, not significant), mobility or walking speed. An effect size of about 0.5 is a medium change; 0.7 is medium to large.
all_events.caution: Better balance on a test is not the same as fewer falls. Balance results differed a lot between trials, mood and sleep were self-reported, and some trials had unclear risk of bias. Versus other exercise, yoga did not win for balance, mobility or walking speed. The large SAGE trial (University of Sydney, Lancet Healthy Longevity 2025;6:100749, 700 people aged 60+, mean age 67, 81% women) tested 80 one-hour, twice-weekly Iyengar-based classes over 12 months, run online because of COVID-19, against seated relaxation yoga. The active yoga group had MORE falls: 0.87 vs 0.64 falls per person per year (about 33% more), with no rise in falls that caused injury, although balance confidence and weekly exercise went up.
