The researchers said Iyengar yoga should not be recommended as a fall prevention strategy. Do not claim yoga prevents falls. Cochrane 2019 (Sherrington, 108 trials, 23,407 people) found balance and functional exercise lowered the rate of falls by 24%. Minor harms in the yoga trials: a groin muscle strain, a fall during class, some muscle pain.
all_events.citation: Sivaramakrishnan D, Fitzsimons C, Kelly P, Ludwig K, Mutrie N, Saunders DH, Baker G. The effects of yoga compared to active and inactive controls on physical function and health related quality of life in older adults: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act. 2019;16(1):33. doi:10.1186/s12966-019-0789-2. PMID 30953508.

all_events.topic: Bone density: 12 asanas, 12 minutes a day
all_events.title_line: Columbia University (Dr Loren Fishman) and partners · New York · 2016
all_events.headline: 12 asanas, 12 minutes a day: in a small early study, spine bone density went up.
all_events.meaning: Holding asanas puts gentle load on bones. Early signs say this may help thin bones, but the proof is still weak.
all_events.details: Ten-year study (2005 to 2015). 741 volunteers found online got a free DVD of 12 asanas, each held 30 seconds, about 12 minutes a day: Vrksasana, Trikonasana, Virabhadrasana II, Parsvakonasana, Parivrtta Trikonasana, Salabhasana, Setu Bandhasana, Supta Padangusthasana I and II, Marichyasana II (straight-leg twist), Matsyendrasana (bent-knee twist) and Savasana. 227 people practised more than every other day (202 women, mean age 68.2; 83% had osteoporosis or osteopenia). Bone scans (DXA) before yoga were compared with scans after starting yoga, so each person was compared with themselves. Before yoga, spine bone density was falling by 0.0036 g/cm2 per month. After starting yoga, it rose by 0.0029 g/cm2 per month (P = .005). The femur gain was borderline (P = .053 in the abstract). The total hip gain was not statistically significant. Across more than 90,000 hours of practice, no yoga-related fractures or serious injuries were reported.
all_events.caution: Weak evidence: no separate control group, self-selected internet volunteers (many already did yoga), self-reported practice, and only 27 (spine), 16 (total hip) and 14 (femur) people had full 2-year before-and-after scan data. The paper's own title says 'reverses', but the slide must say 'an early study found', never 'proven' or 'reverses'. SAFETY: a Mayo Clinic case series (Sfeir et al., Eur J Phys Rehabil Med 2018;54(6):947-951) reported 9 people (8 women, median age 66) with spine compression fractures after yoga spinal flexion (forward-bending) exercises. People with osteoporosis should avoid deep forward folds and forced twists and should ask a doctor before practising. Many Ashtanga primary series asanas are deep forward bends.
all_events.citation: Lu YH, Rosner B, Chang G, Fishman LM. Twelve-Minute Daily Yoga Regimen Reverses Osteoporotic Bone Loss. Top Geriatr Rehabil. 2016;32(2):81-87 (online 5 Nov 2015). doi:10.1097/TGR.0000000000000085. PMID 27226695. PMCID PMC4851231.

all_events.topic: Longevity: the sit and rise from the floor test
all_events.title_line: CLINIMEX Exercise Medicine Clinic, Rio de Janeiro · Brazil · 2025
all_events.headline: Can you sit on the floor and stand up with no hands? Adults who could had far better 12-year survival.
all_events.meaning: Rising from the floor needs strength, balance and flexibility, which asana trains. This simple skill is linked to a longer life.
all_events.details: Prospective cohort of 4,282 adults aged 46 to 75 (68% men), tested between 1998 and 2023 at an exercise medicine clinic in Rio de Janeiro. The sitting-rising test: sit down on the floor and stand back up. Sitting down scores up to 5 points and standing up scores up to 5, for 10 in total. Lose 1 point for each support used (hand or knee) and 0.5 for wobbling. People were followed for a median of 12.3 years, and 665 died of natural causes (15.5%). Death rate: 3.7% for a perfect score of 10, 11.1% for a score of 8, and 42.1% for scores of 0 to 4. After adjusting for age, sex, body mass index (BMI) and health conditions, the lowest scorers had 3.8 times the risk of natural death and 6.0 times the risk of heart-related death compared with perfect scorers. An earlier study by the same team (Brito et al., Eur J Prev Cardiol 2014;21(7):892-8; 2,002 adults aged 51 to 80, median 6.3 years) found each 1 point higher score was linked to 21% better survival.
all_events.caution: Observational: it shows a link, not that practice makes people live longer. This is not a yoga study. People were volunteers at one exercise clinic with no major limits for fitness testing, so results may not fit everyone. COVID and accidental or other outside-cause deaths were excluded. People with knee or hip problems, a joint replacement, or poor balance should not try the test alone: use a wall or a helper. Phrase slides around 'staying alive and well', not death counts.
all_events.citation: Araujo CGS, de Souza e Silva CG, Myers J, Laukkanen JA, Ramos PS, Ricardo DR. Sitting-rising test scores predict natural and cardiovascular causes of deaths in middle-aged and older men and women. Eur J Prev Cardiol. 2025 (print 2026;33(12):2170-2178). doi:10.1093/eurjpc/zwaf325. PMID 40569873.

all_events.title_line: University of Pittsburgh · USA · 2011
all_events.headline: How fast older adults walked predicted how long they lived, in a study of 34,485 people.
all_events.meaning: Walking uses your heart, lungs, nerves and muscles together, so walking speed works like a simple health check as you age.
all_events.details: Pooled analysis of 9 cohort studies (data collected 1986 to 2000) with 34,485 adults aged 65 and over living at home (mean age 73.5, 59.6% women), followed for 6 to 21 years (mean 12.2 years). Average walking speed was 0.92 metres per second. Every 0.1 m/s faster was linked to a 12% lower risk of death (hazard ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.87 to 0.90). At age 75, predicted 10-year survival ranged from 19% (slowest walkers) to 87% (fastest walkers) in men, and from 35% to 91% in women. About 0.8 m/s matched average life expectancy. People walking 1.0 m/s or faster (about 3.6 km/h) lived longer than expected for their age and sex. Age, sex and walking speed together predicted survival as well as age, sex plus a list of illnesses, smoking history, blood pressure, body weight (BMI) and past hospital stays.
all_events.caution: Observational: the authors say it cannot show cause and effect. Walking speed is a marker of health, not proof that training it adds years. This is not a yoga study. A 2019 meta-analysis of 22 yoga trials in older adults (Sivaramakrishnan, Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act) found yoga helped balance, leg strength and flexibility, but found no clear gain in walking speed, so do not claim yoga makes you walk faster or live longer.
all_events.citation: Studenski S, Perera S, Patel K, et al. Gait speed and survival in older adults. JAMA. 2011;305(1):50-58. doi:10.1001/jama.2010.1923. PMID 21205966.

all_events.title_line: AIIMS Rishikesh, India · Journal of Glaucoma · 2021
all_events.headline: Daily yoga breathing for 6 months lowered eye pressure in people with glaucoma, more than eye drops alone.
all_events.meaning: Glaucoma can harm sight through high eye pressure. Daily pranayama helped lower it more, next to eye drops, never instead.
all_events.details: Randomized controlled trial at AIIMS Rishikesh, India. 90 people over age 40 with primary open-angle glaucoma (180 eyes), split into 2 groups of 45. Everyone kept using their eye drops. One group also did yogic pranayama (Anulom Vilom, alternate nostril breathing) plus belly (diaphragm) breathing, 30 minutes every day for 6 months: 4 weeks with a teacher, then at home. The other group used eye drops only (wait-list group). Eye pressure was checked at the start and after 1, 3 and 6 months. Breathing group: right eye 20.85 to 14.90 mmHg, left eye 20.30 to 14.25 mmHg, about 6 mmHg lower. The eye drops only group also went down: right eye 19.51 to 15.76, left eye 19.32 to 15.32, about 4 mmHg lower. So the breathing added about 2 mmHg of extra drop. The difference between groups was significant (P<0.001). 9 people (4 breathing, 5 control) missed some check-ups.
all_events.caution: The authors say clearly: breathing is an add-on, not a swap for eye drops or surgery. Never stop glaucoma medicine. Small study at one hospital, not blinded, eye pressure checked once a day only, no eye nerve scans or vision field tests. A 2023 commentary in the Indian Journal of Ophthalmology warns that breath holding may raise eye pressure, and head-down asana like headstand can double it. People with glaucoma should keep the breath smooth, skip long holds, and ask their eye doctor before inversions.
all_events.citation: Udenia H, Mittal S, Agrawal A, Singh A, Singh A, Mittal SK. Yogic Pranayama and Diaphragmatic Breathing: Adjunct Therapy for Intraocular Pressure in Patients With Primary Open-angle Glaucoma: A Randomized Controlled Trial. J Glaucoma. 2021;30(2):115-123. doi:10.1097/IJG.0000000000001697. PMID 33955942. Safety note: Commentary: The impact of yoga practice on glaucoma. Indian J Ophthalmol. 2023. PMID 37203028.

all_events.title_line: AIIMS New Delhi and Magdeburg University, Germany · 2018
all_events.headline: 21 days of breathing and meditation, on top of eye drops, lowered eye pressure about one third in glaucoma patients.
all_events.meaning: Stress is linked to glaucoma. Daily breathing and meditation lowered eye pressure and the stress hormone cortisol together.
all_events.details: Randomized controlled trial, Journal of Glaucoma. 90 people with open-angle glaucoma (180 eyes, age over 45). One group did breathing exercises plus mindfulness meditation with a trained yoga teacher, 60 minutes every morning for 21 days, and kept using their eye drops. The other group kept their eye drops and waited, with no meditation. Meditators' eye pressure: right eye 18.8 to 12.7 mmHg, left eye 19.0 to 13.1 mmHg (about 32% lower). Stress hormone cortisol fell from 497.3 to 392.3 ng/mL. Feel-good beta-endorphin rose from 38.4 to 52.7 pg/mL. Nerve growth protein BDNF rose from 56.1 to 83.9 ng/mL. Quality of life went up. Press release: 3 in 4 meditators had a 25% drop in eye pressure. Lead doctor Tanuj Dada: "Mindfulness meditation is easy to do, even by patients who are elderly and bedridden." A second AIIMS trial (American Journal of Ophthalmology 2021, doi:10.1016/j.ajo.2020.10.012) took 60 patients whose pressure stayed high on full eye drops and who were already booked for surgery. 30 of them added 45 minutes of meditation a day for 3 weeks: pressure went from 20.16 to 15.05 mmHg. The 30 on eye drops only went from 21.2 to 20.0 mmHg.
all_events.caution: Short trials (3 weeks), small groups, all from the same research team in New Delhi. Meditation was added to eye drops, not used instead of them. Nobody has yet shown it saves sight over many years. Safety: in headstand (Sirsasana), eye pressure doubled in 75 yoga practitioners (Ophthalmology 2006), so people with glaucoma should ask their eye doctor before upside-down asana.
all_events.citation: Dada T, Mittal D, Mohanty K, Faiq MA, Bhat MA, Yadav RK, Sihota R, Sidhu T, Velpandian T, Kalaivani M, Pandey RM, Gao Y, Sabel BA, Dada R. Mindfulness Meditation Reduces Intraocular Pressure, Lowers Stress Biomarkers and Modulates Gene Expression in Glaucoma: A Randomized Controlled Trial. J Glaucoma. 2018;27(12):1061-1067. doi:10.1097/IJG.0000000000001088. PMID 30256277. Second trial: Dada T et al. Am J Ophthalmol. 2021;223:308-321. doi:10.1016/j.ajo.2020.10.012. PMID 33393484. Safety: Baskaran M et al. Ophthalmology. 2006;113(8):1327-32. doi:10.1016/j.ophtha.2006.02.063. PMID 16806478. Press release: medicalxpress.com/news/2018-11-meditationan-effective-therapy-eye-pressure.html

all_events.title_line: Mount Sinai, New York · 2015, and Sankara Nethralaya, Chennai · 2006
all_events.headline: Headstand doubled eye pressure. In downward dog asana, eye pressure rose by about three quarters within two minutes.
all_events.meaning: In the downward dog study, pressure was normal 2 minutes after sitting up. Glaucoma? Ask your eye doctor before inversions.
all_events.details: Study 1, PLOS ONE 2015 (Jasien, Jonas, de Moraes, Ritch; New York Eye and Ear Infirmary of Mount Sinai). Design: one center, observational, no control treatment. 20 people: 10 with glaucoma (median age 62, 9 women) and 10 healthy (median age 36, 8 women). Each held 4 head-down asanas for 2 minutes. Eye pressure rose within 1 minute in every asana, in both groups. Downward dog (Adho Mukha Svanasana): glaucoma 17 to 28 mmHg, healthy 17 to 29 mmHg (average rise 72% and 79%). Standing forward bend (Uttanasana): 17 to 27 and 18 to 26 (61% and 48%). Plough (Halasana): 18 to 24 and 18 to 22 (33% and 28%). Legs up the wall (Viparita Karani): 17 to 21 in both (23% and 25%). Pressure went back to normal within 2 minutes of sitting up. Rise was about the same in glaucoma and healthy eyes. Study 2, Ophthalmology 2006 (Baskaran and team, Sankara Nethralaya, Chennai, India). Design: observational case series. 75 experienced practitioners from a yoga training institute (50 Indian, 25 Caucasian). In headstand (Sirsasana), eye pressure went up by about 15 mmHg right away and about 16 mmHg after 5 minutes: 2 times the starting level. It stayed high while they held the asana, in all age groups.
all_events.caution: These are short spikes measured in small, non-randomized studies. Long-term harm in healthy eyes is not proven. The Glaucoma Research Foundation says the safest way for people with glaucoma is to avoid inversions, and to tell their yoga teacher so the practice can be changed. One case report (Indian Journal of Ophthalmology 2009, PubMed 19075418) describes a 55-year-old man on blood thinners, with a past lung clot, who lost vision in one eye from a blocked eye vein after headstand. Very relevant for Ashtanga, where downward dog comes in every sun salutation.
all_events.citation: Jasien JV, Jonas JB, de Moraes CG, Ritch R. Intraocular Pressure Rise in Subjects with and without Glaucoma during Four Common Yoga Positions. PLoS One. 2015;10(12):e0144505. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0144505. PMID 26698309. AND Baskaran M, Raman K, Ramani KK, Roy J, Vijaya L, Badrinath SS. Intraocular pressure changes and ocular biometry during Sirsasana (headstand posture) in yoga practitioners. Ophthalmology. 2006;113(8):1327-32. doi:10.1016/j.ophtha.2006.02.063. PMID 16806478.

all_events.title_line: University of Patanjali, Haridwar, India · Indian Journal of Ophthalmology · 2023
all_events.headline: A review of 6 studies: slow breathing and candle gazing helped lower eye pressure, head-down asanas raised it.
all_events.meaning: For glaucoma, calm breathing can help next to eye drops, not instead of them. Head-down asanas need a doctor's okay.
all_events.details: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 6 studies (2007 to 2021, 234 adults aged 23 to 77). It pooled 3 randomized trials with 212 glaucoma patients in India and Egypt. They did pranayama with belly breathing and Nadi Shodhana (30 minutes a day for 6 months), breath-focused meditation (45 minutes a day for 6 weeks), or Jyoti-trataka, steady gazing at a candle flame (55 minutes a day for 1 month). Eye pressure dropped more in the yoga groups than in the control groups: right eye by 1.50 mmHg more (95% CI 0.17 to 2.82), left eye by 1.30 mmHg more (95% CI 0.32 to 2.28). The trataka trial (62 glaucoma patients with type 2 diabetes, half did yoga plus medicine, half medicine only) also saw lower blood pressure, pulse, breathing rate and fasting blood sugar. The head-down evidence came from 1 study of 20 people and 2 single-patient reports. In the study, Adho Mukha Svanasana, Uttanasana, Halasana and Viparita Karani all raised eye pressure within 1 minute, and it went back to normal within 2 minutes of sitting up.
all_events.caution: Only 3 small trials, not blinded, and their results varied a lot (I2 = 76% and 93%). The drop was small (about 1.3 to 1.5 mmHg). The authors say yoga is not a substitute for drugs, glaucoma patients should avoid head-down asanas (Sirsasana, Adho Mukha Svanasana, Uttanasana, Halasana, Viparita Karani), and pranayama with breath holding may raise eye pressure. A 2026 systematic review of 14 studies (Abraham, George and Bhat, Advances in Mind-Body Medicine) agreed: strong support for meditation and pranayama as helpers in glaucoma, but limited and unclear evidence for dry eye and short sight (myopia).
all_events.citation: Chetry D, Singh J, Chhetri A, Katiyar VK, Singh DS. Effect of yoga on intra-ocular pressure in patients with glaucoma: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Indian J Ophthalmol. 2023 May;71(5):1757-1765. doi:10.4103/ijo.IJO_2054_22. PMID 37203026. PMC10391478. Also: Abraham L, George S, Bhat R. Yoga for Eye Disorders: A Systematic Review. Adv Mind Body Med. 2026 May;40(3):24-31. PMID 41217898.

all_events.title_line: Swami Vivekananda Yoga Research Foundation, Bangalore · 2006
all_events.headline: Computer workers who did yoga for 60 days reported 32% less eye discomfort. The group without yoga reported 43% more.
all_events.meaning: Long screen hours tire the eyes. Daily asana, breathing, eye exercises and rest helped these computer workers' eyes feel more comfortable.
all_events.details: Randomized trial in Head & Face Medicine. 291 people at a software company in Bangalore, aged 21 to 49, who used a computer at least 6 hours a day, were split by chance into yoga (146) and wait-list (145). The yoga group practiced 1 hour a day, 5 days a week, for 60 days: 15 minutes asana, 10 minutes pranayama, 10 minutes joint loosening, 10 minutes trataka (moving the eyes in 8 directions and gazing at a flame), and 15 minutes guided relaxation. The wait-list group did their usual free-time activities for an hour a day. A 12-question survey rated dryness, irritation, burning, redness and light sensitivity from 0 to 3. Average score: yoga group 1.03 to 0.70 (32% lower). Wait-list group 1.05 to 1.50 (43% higher). These percents are worked out from the paper's averages, for the people who finished. Two smaller studies that were not randomized point the same way: 32 optometry students in Bengaluru, 16 doing yoga eye exercises for up to 6 weeks, had lower eye fatigue scores while the other 16 got higher scores (Int J Yoga 2020, PMID 32030026); 40 nursing students in Korea, 20 doing palming, blinking and gazing exercises 60 minutes twice a week for 8 weeks, had lower eye fatigue scores than the 20 who did not (J Phys Ther Sci 2016, PMID 27390422).
all_events.caution: Many people dropped out: only 62 of 146 (yoga) and 55 of 145 (wait-list) finished, mainly because of busy work schedules. Results count only those who finished. Scores were self-reported, with no eye tests like tear film checks. Evidence for real dry eye disease is still limited. Yoga does not replace glasses, eye drops or an eye doctor. If eyes stay dry, red or painful, see an eye doctor.
all_events.citation: Telles S, Naveen KV, Dash M, Deginal R, Manjunath NK. Effect of yoga on self-rated visual discomfort in computer users. Head Face Med. 2006;2:46. doi:10.1186/1746-160X-2-46. PMID 17140457.

all_events.title_line: University of Birmingham, UK · 2001
all_events.headline: Rowers did 30 hard breaths, twice a day. After 11 weeks, their 5 km row was 36 seconds faster.
all_events.meaning: Breathing muscles can be trained, like leg muscles. In this small study, it helped rowers get faster than a fake-training group.
all_events.details: Placebo-controlled trial. 14 female competitive rowers, tested on a rowing machine (not on water) before and after 11 weeks. Training group (7 rowers): 30 breaths in, twice a day, against a resistance equal to 50% of their maximum breathing-in pressure, using a breathing trainer device. Placebo group (7 rowers): same device, 60 easy breaths once a day at only 15%. Results: breathing-in strength rose 45% in the training group (placebo: 5%). Distance in a 6-minute all-out row went up 3.5% (placebo: 1.6%). 5,000 m time dropped by 36 seconds, 3.1% (placebo: 11 seconds, 0.9%), so about 25 seconds more than the placebo group. Breathing muscle tiredness after the hard 6-minute row shrank from an 11.2% loss of strength to only 3.0%.
all_events.citation: Volianitis S, McConnell AK, Koutedakis Y, McNaughton L, Backx K, Jones DA. Inspiratory muscle training improves rowing performance. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2001;33(5):803-809. doi:10.1097/00005768-200105000-00020. PMID 11323552.
all_events.caution: Very small study (14 rowers, 7 per group). The abstract does not say the groups were randomized. Tests were on a rowing machine. They used a breathing trainer device, not yoga pranayama, so do not claim yoga breathing gives the same 36 seconds. Safe slide wording: 'studies found breathing muscles can be trained'. People with heart or lung problems should ask a doctor before using a breathing trainer.

all_events.title_line: University of Birmingham, UK · 2002
all_events.headline: Six weeks of breathing muscle training helped trained cyclists finish a 40 km lab race almost 2 minutes faster.
all_events.meaning: Breathing muscles can be trained. After training, hard riding felt easier on breath and legs, and the riders went faster.
all_events.details: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized trial at the University of Birmingham, UK. 16 trained male cyclists (fitness VO2max about 64 mL/kg/min) were split at random into a real breathing-muscle training group (using a pressure-threshold breathing device) and a fake-training (placebo) group for 6 weeks. Speed was tested on a lab bike, in time trials equal to 20 km and 40 km. After training, the real group finished the 20 km trial 66 seconds faster (3.8%) and the 40 km trial 115 seconds faster (4.6%) than the placebo group. Lung function tests did not change, but the breathing muscles worked better. In a hard step-by-step bike test, riders also felt less effort: breathing effort 16% lower and leg effort 18% lower than placebo (Borg CR10 scale). A companion paper by the same team, with the same 16 riders (Med Sci Sports Exerc 2002), found the training also cut breathing muscle tiredness after the time trials.
all_events.citation: Romer LM, McConnell AK, Jones DA. Effects of inspiratory muscle training on time-trial performance in trained cyclists. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2002;20(7):547-562. doi:10.1080/026404102760000053. PMID 12166881. Companion: Romer LM, McConnell AK, Jones DA. Inspiratory muscle fatigue in trained cyclists: effects of inspiratory muscle training. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2002;34(5):785-792. doi:10.1097/00005768-200205000-00010. PMID 11984296.
all_events.caution: Small study (16 men only). Lab bike time trials, not a real road race. Lung function did NOT change, so do not say 'bigger lungs'; say 'breathing muscles worked better'. Training used a breathing device, not pranayama, so do not say yoga breathing gives the same result.

all_events.topic: Athletes and everyone: breath training review
all_events.title_line: ETH Zurich, Switzerland · 2012
all_events.headline: A review of 46 studies found breathing muscle training improved endurance in healthy people. Less fit people gained more.
all_events.meaning: You do not need to be an athlete. Less fit people and longer efforts showed bigger gains from breathing muscle training.
all_events.details: Systematic review and meta-analysis by ETH Zurich, published in Sports Medicine (2012). It pooled 46 original studies of healthy people who trained their breathing muscles with trainer devices. Sports studied included rowing, running, swimming and cycling. Less fit people improved more: about 6.0% more improvement for every 10 mL/kg/min lower fitness (VO2max). Longer efforts improved more: +0.4% for every extra minute of test time. 'How long can you last' tests at a steady pace showed about 16% more improvement than standard step-up tests, and interval step-up tests about 18.5% more. Race-style time trials showed no more change than standard step-up tests. The type of sport made no difference. A meta-analysis of 8 controlled trials confirmed a real improvement. Training both breathing in and breathing out may work best (+12.8% more than training breathing in only, but based on only 6 studies). A second review (University of British Columbia, 2013, 21 randomized trials in athletes) also found breathing muscle training improved sport performance, such as time trials and endurance time.
all_events.citation: Illi SK, Held U, Frank I, Spengler CM. Effect of respiratory muscle training on exercise performance in healthy individuals: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. 2012;42(8):707-724. doi:10.1007/BF03262290. PMID 22765281. Supporting: HajGhanbari B, Yamabayashi C, Buna TR, et al. Effects of respiratory muscle training on performance in athletes: a systematic review with meta-analyses. J Strength Cond Res. 2013;27(6):1643-1663. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e318269f73f. PMID 22836606.
all_events.caution: The 16% and 18.5% numbers compare types of tests. They do not mean everyone got 16% better. Race-style time trials showed smaller changes. Most of the pooled studies were small. Studies used breathing trainer devices, not yoga breathing (pranayama), so do not claim the same result for pranayama.

all_events.title_line: Paula Radcliffe, UK runner · London Marathon 2003
all_events.headline: Paula Radcliffe learned she had asthma at about 14. Later she set a marathon world record that stood 16 years.
all_events.meaning: Asthma did not stop her. The right medicine, a simple lung check, and her doctor's plan let her train hard.
all_events.details: She was diagnosed with asthma at about 14, after getting dizzy and short of breath after training, and once blacking out in training (World Athletics interview, 2019). Healthline calls it exercise-induced asthma. One main trigger was oilseed rape, a yellow crop in the fields near her new home in Bedfordshire, plus more pollution in a more built-up area. Her family doctor gave her inhalers and a peak flow meter, a tube that measures how hard and fast you can blow out in one breath. It showed her when she needed to raise her preventer inhaler dose. Later, sports science teams found which pollens set off her asthma, so she could avoid those training areas. Her doctor told her: 'This isn't going to stop you doing any of your sport, you're just going to have to learn to control it' (Healthline). She set the women's marathon world record, 2:15:25, at the 2003 London Marathon. It stood 16 years, until Brigid Kosgei broke it in 2019. She also won the marathon at the 2005 World Championships in Helsinki. Her advice: 'control your asthma and not let it control you.' She says a marathon runner breathes in as much air in three hours as an inactive person does over two days. Bonus fact: a 2012 review by Ken Fitch (University of Western Australia, British Journal of Sports Medicine) looked at data from the last 5 Olympic Games. It found asthma or 'twitchy airways' (airway hyper-responsiveness) is the most common long-term medical condition in Olympic athletes, about 8%. Athletes with it have consistently done better than their peers, and research suggests this is not because of their medicine.
all_events.citation: World Athletics. 'Radcliffe: from elite athlete to clean air advocate.' worldathletics.org, 1 March 2019. Healthline. 'Famous Athletes with Asthma.' healthline.com/health/famous-athletes-with-asthma. Fitch KD. An overview of asthma and airway hyper-responsiveness in Olympic athletes. Br J Sports Med. 2012;46(6):413-416. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2011-090814. PMID 22228581.
all_events.caution: Asthma is serious. Breathing practice supports, but never replaces, an inhaler or a doctor's plan. Never suggest students stop or change their medicine on their own; inhaler doses follow the doctor's plan. Do not claim asthma makes you faster: Fitch says the 'did better' finding is not explained by the medicine, and the cause is unknown. Fitch also suggests years of hard endurance training may help cause asthma that starts later in some athletes, so do not claim hard training protects the lungs. This is one person's story plus an observational review, not a trial. Alternative champion if needed: Jackie Joyner-Kersee (severe asthma found while a UCLA athlete; 6 Olympic medals: 3 gold, 1 silver, 2 bronze, per Healthline; heptathlon world record 7,291 points, Seoul 1988).

all_events.topic: Athletes: credits yoga for a long career
all_events.title_line: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, NBA · 1969 to 1989
all_events.headline: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar says yoga helped him play 20 NBA seasons, until age 42, with few injuries.
all_events.meaning: He calls yoga one of the reasons, with martial arts and training. One person's story, but a strong example of steady practice.
all_events.details: On his website he writes: 'Yoga is one of the reasons that I was able to play professional basketball as long as I did with as few injuries as I had.' He says yoga has 'worked for me for over 45 years.' Before yoga he had lower back pain. He says his posture got better and 'my overall health improved significantly.' Sources differ on when he started: his site says 'since high school', while Wikipedia (citing a yoga expo article) says he began in 1976 in Los Angeles. He also credited martial arts training with Bruce Lee and a year-round fitness plan he began at age 26. Career facts (Britannica): born April 16, 1947; 20 NBA seasons, 1969-70 to 1988-89; retired in 1989 at age 42 with 38,387 points, the NBA all-time scoring record until LeBron James passed it in February 2023; record six-time MVP.
all_events.citation: Abdul-Jabbar K. 'Fit after 50: Staying Flexible With Yoga.' kareemabduljabbar.com. Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Kareem Abdul-Jabbar' biography, britannica.com/biography/Kareem-Abdul-Jabbar.
all_events.caution: One person's story, not a study: say 'he says yoga helped', never 'yoga made him' or 'yoga prevents injuries'. He also credits martial arts and conditioning, so do not present yoga as the only reason. Do not state 'since high school' as fact; sources disagree (high school vs 1976). Do not say he is the all-time top scorer today; LeBron James passed him in 2023. Do not name the hot-yoga brand or its founder (legal scandal), and leave out his political writing.

all_events.topic: Magical but true: breath and the immune system
all_events.title_line: Radboud University Medical Center · Nijmegen, Netherlands · 2014
all_events.headline: Men trained 10 days in breathing, cold and meditation felt less sick after a shot of dead germ parts.
all_events.meaning: Breathing may change how the body's defense system reacts. One small study in healthy young men found signs of this.
all_events.details: Design: randomized controlled trial, published in PNAS (May 2014). 24 healthy young men (median age 24 in the trained group, 22 in the control group, all aged 19 to 27). 12 men were trained for 10 days in the Wim Hof method: 4 days in Poland, then practice at home. The training had three parts: breathing (many fast deep breaths, then holding the breath), cold (ice water at 0 to 1°C, snow, hiking in the cold) and meditation. 12 men got no training. On the test day, the trained men did only the breathing exercises. Then all 24 got an injection of a tiny dose of dead bacteria parts (E. coli endotoxin, 2 ng per kg), which normally causes fever and flu-like feelings for a few hours. Results: before the injection, the trained men already had about 3 times more adrenaline in their blood (1.02 vs 0.35 nmol/L). 30 minutes into the breathing, it rose to 2.08. The authors wrote that mainly the breathing caused this rise. Their calming immune signal IL-10 was 194% higher. Inflammation signals were lower: TNF-alpha 53% lower, IL-6 57% lower, IL-8 51% lower. Flu-like symptoms (headache, nausea, shivering, muscle and back pain) were 56% lower at their worst. In the untrained group, temperature rose by about 1.9°C on average at its highest. In the trained group the rise was smaller and went back to normal sooner. During the breath holds, blood oxygen dipped to about 50% for around 10 seconds. Lead scientist Dr. Matthijs Kox: "The trained men produced more of the hormone epinephrine as a result of the techniques they had learned." Slide line idea: 12 men. 10 days of training. Inflammation signals about 50% lower. Flu-like symptoms 56% lower at their worst.
all_events.caution: Small study: 24 healthy young men only, 12 per group. The 10-day training mixed breathing, ice cold water and meditation, so no one can say breath alone did it. The authors said their design cannot show which part of the breathing caused the effect. The researchers said it has not yet been tested in patients. Safety: the fast breathing plus breath hold method dropped blood oxygen to about 50% for short moments and can cause fainting. Never practice it in water, in a bath, while driving or while standing. Ask a doctor first if pregnant or living with heart problems, epilepsy or high blood pressure. This is not Ashtanga pranayama. Say so clearly on the slide.
all_events.citation: Kox M, van Eijk LT, Zwaag J, van den Wildenberg J, Sweep FC, van der Hoeven JG, Pickkers P. Voluntary activation of the sympathetic nervous system and attenuation of the innate immune response in humans. Proc Natl Acad Sci USA. 2014;111(20):7379-7384. doi:10.1073/pnas.1322174111. PMID 24799686. Press release: Radboud University, "Modulating your own immune response" (ScienceDaily, 5 May 2014, https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2014/05/140505155210.htm).

all_events.topic: Magical but true: breath and body heat
all_events.title_line: Harvard Medical School team (Herbert Benson) · Himalayas, India · 1982
all_events.headline: 3 monks warmed their fingers and toes by up to 8.3°C during a breath and focus practice.
all_events.meaning: Real numbers, not legends: fingers and toes got warmer, but readings stayed between 22°C and 33°C, a normal range.
all_events.details: Design: small field study of 3 people (listed as case reports), published in Nature on 21 January 1982. Herbert Benson (Harvard Medical School) and colleagues from the USA and India tested 3 expert monks who practiced g Tum-mo (inner heat) meditation, a practice that uses breath and focus. Testing was done in February 1981 in the Himalayas of northern India. Results: finger and toe temperature rose by as much as 8.3°C. Skin at the navel and lower back rose about 1.9°C. Core body temperature (rectal) did not rise. A 2013 paper that looked back at this data notes the finger and toe readings stayed between 22°C and 33°C, which is a normal range. Follow-up study: National University of Singapore team (Kozhevnikov and colleagues, PLOS ONE, 2013) tested 10 expert meditators (7 women, ages 25 to 52, 6 to 32 years of practice) in remote mountain monasteries in Qinghai, China, above 4,200 m, in rooms near 0°C. Finger warming there came mostly from tensing the hands and pressing the fists into the hip crease, so the team measured armpit temperature instead. During the "Forceful Breath" practice with visualization, the 6 meditators who did it reached an average of 37.6°C and up to 38.3°C (slight fever zone). The biggest rise was 2.2°C. 11 Western yoga and martial arts practitioners in New Jersey, USA (10 women, ages 46 to 70, 7 to 30 years of practice) copied only the breathing, with no visualization. Their rises were smaller and stayed in the normal range. The team concluded the breathing makes the heat and the visualization helps keep it going longer. Slide line idea: 3 monks. One inner heat practice. Fingers and toes up to 8.3°C warmer. Published in Nature, 1982.
all_events.caution: Only 3 people, tested in 1981, never repeated in a large trial. Fingers and toes warmed but stayed in a normal range (22 to 33°C). The 2013 team found finger warming came mostly from tensing the hands, and notes that people using biofeedback or hypnosis (no meditation) have warmed their fingers by up to 11.7°C, so do not say the mind alone did it. Posts saying "17 degrees" are wrong: the top rise was 8.3°C (about 15°F). The 2013 team says steaming wet sheets do not prove higher body heat. Do not call it a superpower. Forceful breath holding is not for beginners, pregnant women, or people with heart problems or high blood pressure without a doctor's advice. For China-facing channels, describe the settings simply as "monks in the Himalayas of India" and "mountain monasteries in Qinghai, China", and do not name any political or religious leaders linked to the study.
all_events.citation: Benson H, Lehmann JW, Malhotra MS, Goldman RF, Hopkins J, Epstein MD. Body temperature changes during the practice of g Tum-mo yoga. Nature. 1982;295(5846):234-236. doi:10.1038/295234a0. PMID 7035966. Follow-up: Kozhevnikov M, Elliott J, Shephard J, Gramann K. Neurocognitive and somatic components of temperature increases during g-Tummo meditation: legend and reality. PLoS One. 2013;8(3):e58244. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0058244 (open access: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0058244).

all_events.topic: Magical but true: your nose makes its own gas
all_events.title_line: Karolinska Hospital and Institute · Stockholm, Sweden · 2002
all_events.headline: In 10 people, humming made nitric oxide gas in the nose 15 times higher than quiet breathing out.
all_events.meaning: Your nose makes a gas that helps blood vessels open. Nose breathing carries it to the lungs. Humming let out far more.
all_events.details: Design: small lab study by Eddie Weitzberg and Jon Lundberg at Karolinska in Stockholm, published in the American Journal of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine (15 July 2002). 10 healthy people. Scientists measured nitric oxide (NO) in air breathed out through the nose. NO is a gas made in the sinuses. It helps blood vessels open, and scientists think it may help keep germs down. They compared humming with quiet breathing out at the same air speed. Result: NO was 15 times higher during humming. Why: the scientists think the buzzing air moves air in and out of the sinuses. In a simple model of the nose and sinus, buzzing air made gas move between them much faster. Background 1 (Nature Medicine, 1995): Lundberg's team showed the sinuses make very high levels of NO, and suggested it may help keep the sinuses clean. Background 2, nose vs mouth (Acta Physiologica Scandinavica, 1996): in 6 of 8 healthy people, oxygen measured through the skin was 10% higher during nose breathing than during mouth breathing. The same paper says nose NO reaches the lungs when we breathe in, most of all through the nose. Link for Ashtanga: in every asana the breath goes in and out through the nose; humming is the sound of bhramari (bee breath). Slide line idea: Hum for one breath. In a study, the nose let out 15 times more nitric oxide.
all_events.caution: Small studies: 10 people for humming, 8 people for nose vs mouth. They measured gas and oxygen levels, not illness. No study here shows humming prevents colds or sinus infections, so say "raised" or "let out more", never "protects" or "cures". The germ role of NO in the sinuses is an idea from the 1995 paper, not a proven effect. Bhramari itself was not tested; only plain humming was.
all_events.citation: Weitzberg E, Lundberg JO. Humming greatly increases nasal nitric oxide. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2002;166(2):144-145. doi:10.1164/rccm.200202-138BC. PMID 12119224. Also: Lundberg JO, Farkas-Szallasi T, Weitzberg E, et al. High nitric oxide production in human paranasal sinuses. Nat Med. 1995;1(4):370-373. doi:10.1038/nm0495-370. PMID 7585069. Lundberg JO, Settergren G, Gelinder S, Lundberg JM, Alving K, Weitzberg E. Inhalation of nasally derived nitric oxide modulates pulmonary function in humans. Acta Physiol Scand. 1996;158(4):343-347. doi:10.1046/j.1365-201X.1996.557321000.x. PMID 8971255.

all_events.topic: Magical but true: breath-hold world record and the dive reflex
all_events.title_line: Guinness World Records · Opatija, Croatia · 2025
all_events.headline: After 10 minutes of breathing pure oxygen, a Croatian freediver held one breath underwater for 29 minutes 3 seconds.
all_events.meaning: Most people last 30 to 90 seconds. Pure oxygen, years of training and a slow heart made it possible. Never try this.
all_events.details: Event: Vitomir Maričić (Croatia), freediver, held his breath with his face underwater in a pool in Opatija, Croatia, on 14 June 2025: 29 minutes 3 seconds. Guinness title: "Longest time breath held voluntarily underwater (male)". A support team with AIDA freediving judges watched him the whole time. He beat the old record (24 min 37.36 s, Budimir Šobat, Croatia, 2021) by almost 5 minutes. In 1959 the record was 13 min 42.5 s (Robert Foster, USA). Women's record listed by Guinness: Karoline Mariechen Meyer (Brazil), 18 min 32.59 s, Florianopolis, 10 July 2009. He prepared 9 months for it. Before the attempt he breathed 100% pure oxygen for 10 minutes (normal air is 21% oxygen), so this is an oxygen-assisted breath hold. Without pure oxygen, his best is 10 minutes 8 seconds. University of Wollongong physiologists Theresa Larkin and Gregory Peoples (5 Sept 2025): most of us can hold our breath for 30 to 90 seconds; the urge to breathe comes from rising carbon dioxide, not low oxygen; less mental and physical activity, seen as a very low heart rate, lowers how much oxygen the body needs; freedivers train calm with meditation, breath awareness and mindfulness. His words: "After the 20-minute mark, everything became easier, at least mentally." Bonus dive reflex event for a second slide: UC Berkeley, University of Copenhagen and University of Cambridge (Cell, April 2018) measured spleens of 59 Bajau "sea nomads" of Indonesia and 34 Saluan neighbors who do not dive. Bajau spend about 60% of their work day diving for food, to depths over 70 meters, with only a wooden mask. Their spleens were about 50% larger. When a mammal holds its breath underwater, the heart slows and the spleen squeezes out extra oxygen-rich red blood cells: this is the mammalian dive reflex. Bajau who did not dive had spleens as big as Bajau who did, and the study linked the bigger spleen to a gene called PDE10A.
all_events.caution: Always say the record used 10 minutes of pure oxygen first, or the number misleads (his best on normal air is 10 min 8 s). Guinness lists serious risks of very long breath holds: irregular heartbeat, fainting, seizures and brain injury. Wollongong scientists warn that breath holding can quickly cause loss of consciousness, and pure oxygen itself can damage cells. Maričić called it "a very advanced stunt done after years of professional training" that should not be tried without proper guidance and safety. Never practice breath holding in or near water alone; a person can black out without warning. Do not invite followers to try it. In the Bajau study, spleen size seemed to come from genes, not from diving practice.
all_events.citation: Guinness World Records. Longest time breath held voluntarily underwater (male): Vitomir Maričić, 29 min 3 sec, Opatija, Croatia, 14 June 2025 (https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/longest-time-breath-held-voluntarily-(male)); Guinness news, Sept 2025 (https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/news/2025/9/freediver-holds-breath-underwater-for-almost-half-an-hour-to-smash-iconic-record); Guinness, Longest time breath held voluntarily (female) (https://www.guinnessworldrecords.com/world-records/longest-time-breath-held-voluntarily-(female)). Larkin T, Peoples G. The science behind a freediver's 29-minute breath-hold world record. University of Wollongong, 5 Sept 2025 (https://www.uow.edu.au/media/2025/the-science-behind-a-freedivers-29-minute-breath-hold-world-record.php). Bonus: Ilardo MA et al. Physiological and genetic adaptations to diving in sea nomads. Cell. 2018;173(3):569-580. doi:10.1016/j.cell.2018.03.054. PMID 29677510 (UC Berkeley news, 19 April 2018: https://news.berkeley.edu/2018/04/19/enlarged-spleen-key-to-diving-endurance-of-sea-nomads/).

all_events.topic: Magical but true: the diaphragm helps the stomach
all_events.title_line: Medical University of Graz · Austria · 2012
all_events.headline: Four weeks of belly breathing cut the time acid spent in the food pipe almost in half.
all_events.meaning: Your breathing muscle also hugs the valve above your stomach. Training it helped people with acid reflux in a small trial.
all_events.details: Design: randomized controlled trial, published in the American Journal of Gastroenterology (March 2012, online December 2011). 19 adults with a milder type of acid reflux (non-erosive GERD, or a healed sore food pipe), without a large hernia or past surgery: 10 did a belly (diaphragm) breathing training program, 9 did not. Main test after 4 weeks. Results: time with acid in the food pipe (pH under 4) fell from 9.1% to 4.7% of the time measured in the training group; no change in the control group. Quality of life symptom score improved from 13.4 to 10.8 (lower is better); no change in the control group. All 19 were then invited to keep training. After 9 months, the 11 people who kept doing the breathing used much less acid medicine: from 98 to 25 mg per week, and their symptom score fell from 15.1 to 9.7. People who stopped training had no long-term effect. Why it works: the lower part of the diaphragm (the crura) wraps around the valve between the food pipe and the stomach, so training the breathing muscle helps that valve close. Supporting meta-analysis: Ningbo Medical Center Lihuili Hospital, Ningbo, China team (Annals of Palliative Medicine, 2020) pooled 7 studies (3 randomized trials) with 194 patients and 16 healthy volunteers: breathing exercises raised the pressure of this valve, and "to some extent" relieved symptoms. Slide line idea: Your diaphragm is not only for breathing. It also helps close the door above your stomach.
all_events.caution: Small trial (19 people, only 10 trained) with a 4 week main test; the 9 month group chose themselves whether to keep training, so that part has no fair comparison group. The meta-analysis pooled small studies and says only "to some extent". Never stop reflux medicine without a doctor. The popular line "the diaphragm massages your organs" was not measured here; the proven part is the diaphragm helping the stomach valve. Heartburn that lasts, or trouble swallowing, needs a doctor check.
